message: NULL critical section traced to an uninitialised guest heap - RtlCreateHeap is not implemented and six guards already paper over it
note:
Chased the NULL critical section and it led somewhere much better than expected: it is a symptom of the guest HEAP STRUCTURE never being constructed, and that single defect already has SIX hand-written guards papering over it in one function.
HOW: a conditional recomp_where in bridge_RtlEnterCriticalSection, firing only when cs_va == 0, gave identical caller paths every time - sub_001A0B0C <- sub_003437C7 <- sub_003437F3 (operator new). So the NULL lock is the heap's own lock, taken on every allocation. In sub_001A0B0C the lock is fetched as MEM32(esi + 0x580) and passed to ICALL MEM32(0x3C6C5C); esi is the heap object, so the lock pointer is 0 because the heap object is zeroed rather than initialised.
THE REAL DEFECT, and it is already documented six times over in sub_001A0B0C's own guard comments: "on real hardware an initialised-but-empty head points AT ITSELF, which the original CMP_EQ catches. In our build the head reads 0, because the code that should self-initialise it has not run (ebx is the base of a 1MB block from NtAllocateVirtualMemory, so the memory is merely zeroed)." The heap's 128 bucket list heads at heap+0x180 are supposed to be circular lists linked to themselves; ours are all zero. Six guards translate "head == 0" into "empty list" one site at a time, and the NULL lock at +0x580 is the seventh symptom of the same missing construction.
RtlCreateHeap IS NOT IMPLEMENTED ANYWHERE in src/kernel - the only occurrence of the name in the whole tree outside gen/ is a comment in recomp_manual.c. So nothing ever builds that structure; the game gets a 1 MB zeroed block from NtAllocateVirtualMemory and proceeds.
THIS IS THE NEXT TARGET, and it is a fix rather than another guard: construct the guest heap properly - self-link the 128 bucket heads at heap+0x180 (each 8 bytes, next and prev pointing at the head itself), populate the lock at +0x580, and set whatever else sub_001A0B0C reads (+0x1C, +0x30, +0x160 bitmap, +0x60 table). Doing it once should let all six existing guards be deleted, which is the sign it is the right level to fix at. Establish the layout from sub_001A0B0C's own reads plus the ctor path rather than guessing.
Ruled out this turn: the title is NOT bailing out. XapiBootToDash is never called (grep BOOTTODASH -> 0) and there are no RtlRip/assert/panic lines, so the spin is genuine startup work, not a failed startup deciding to quit. That also means the 200-kernel-call "best ever" in this log - which was the XapiBootToDash relaunch loop, 381 nested startup passes and 47.6M dispatches - is not comparable to today's 100, and today's number is worth more than that one.
Still exactly one PsCreateSystemThreadEx call. Signals unchanged and deterministic at 100/195/11/192 across every build this turn; all temporary traces removed; gate still red because it refuses to baseline a hung run.

message: RETRACTION: the guest heap IS correctly constructed - the real anomaly is heap+0x580 being zeroed at runtime
note:
RETRACTING LAST TURN'S HEAP THEORY. I said the guest heap was never constructed and that RtlCreateHeap was missing. Both wrong, and I got the NULL critical section wrong twice on the way. Measured instead of reasoned this time.
WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE. RtlCreateHeap is not a kernel export at all - the Xbox CRT implements its own heap over NtAllocateVirtualMemory, and _heap_init (sub_001A23F3) calls it as sub_001A06E8. That function is present and complete: it self-links the bucket heads at heap+0x180 in a do-while at loc_001A0A3C (MEM32(eax)=eax; MEM32(eax+4)=eax; eax+=8), sets up the large-block head at +0x58/+0x5C, and stores the lock at +0x580.
A probe at sub_001A0B0C's entry confirms the heap is FINE:
  heap=0x00F81000 bucket0.next=0x00F81688 expect=0x00F81180 lock=0x00F81610
  heap=0x00F81000 bucket0.next=0x00F81180 expect=0x00F81180 lock=0x00F81610   <- self-linked, i.e. correctly empty
  heap=0x00F81000 bucket0.next=0x00F81310 expect=0x00F81180 lock=0x00F81610
Bucket 0 is self-linked when the list is empty and points at real in-heap blocks otherwise. That is exactly what an initialised NT-style heap looks like. So the six "the head reads 0 because the code that should self-initialise it has not run" guards in sub_001A0B0C are describing a state this build no longer reaches - they are very likely stale relics from before today's allocator fix. Worth testing by removing them once the boot is further along; do NOT trust their comments as a current description of the heap.
THE ONE REAL ANOMALY, and it is not what I claimed. The lock pointer at heap+0x580 is 0x00F81610 - a valid embedded critical section sitting just past the bucket array - for the first four allocations, and 0x00000000 on the fifth. It starts VALID and gets ZEROED. So the null critical section from last turn is neither "the heap was never built" (my first claim) nor "the game asked for an unserialised heap" (my second) - it is a field being overwritten at runtime. heap+0x580 is immediately after the 128 bucket heads end at 0x580, so an off-by-one bucket write, or a block whose bookkeeping runs one entry long, would land exactly there. That is a concrete corruption target with a fixed guest address, which makes it ideal for the run --watch instrument: watch 0x00F81580:4 and it names the writing instruction.
Also worth noting the arg analysis that misled me: _heap_init pushes six args and I read ebp+0x18 as the lock parameter and concluded the game passes 0. The observed 0x00F81610 says my offset mapping was wrong. Do not re-derive that by counting pushes; probe it.
Not bailing out: XapiBootToDash is still never called and there are no RtlRip/assert lines.
Signals unchanged and deterministic at 100/195/11/192 across every build this turn. All traces removed. Gate still red because it will not baseline a hung run.
NEXT: watch 0x00F81580 to find what zeroes the heap lock pointer, since that is a genuine memory-corruption lead with a stable address rather than another inference.

message: 54 -> 1426 kernel calls: unbounded tree walk was the quiet hang; log cap was hiding the result
note:
54 -> 1,426 KERNEL CALLS. The quiet hang was an unbounded binary-tree walk, and the log cap was hiding most of the win.
FINDING THE HANG. It made no kernel calls and no indirect dispatches - the watchdog fires on the dispatch counter standing still - so nothing a call-site probe can see. Two failed attempts first, recorded so they are not repeated: a probe on sub_00209650's iteration loop (`ebx = MEM32(edi + 4)`) never fired at all, because the callback it dispatches had not returned yet; and a watch on 0x00F81580 fired on the initial mapping write from a system routine and disarmed.
What worked: main.c's watchdog already captures the hung thread's RIP with SuspendThread + GetThreadContext, sitting behind `#if 0` with a comment saying to re-enable it "only to hunt a specific quiet hang, and expect a secondary access violation right after the RIP/stack dump prints". This was exactly that case. Enabled, ran, got RIP RVA 0x6F58E6 -> sub_001186A0+0xD6, plus a stack of sub_0011E7A0 / sub_0011E650 / sub_0011EAAC / sub_0011E980 / sub_002395FE. Re-disabled afterwards. USE THIS FOR ANY QUIET HANG - it is far faster than probing entry/exit of suspected functions, which is what the notes currently advise.
THE BUG. sub_001186A0 is a binary-tree search by child index over a 16-byte-node pool. It is `while (eax != 0x3FFFFFFF)` descending via MEM32(node+0x10) / MEM32(node+0x14), with NO step counter. The manual guard already in that function claims "the iteration cap above bounds how LONG the walk runs but never checks the index itself" - there is no such cap, and that sentence is what sent me looking in the right place. A child link pointing back at an ancestor descends forever with every index perfectly inside the 0x40000 bound, so the existing index guard cannot see it; only a step count can. Added one: a search over at most 0x40000 nodes cannot legitimately take more steps than there are nodes, so past that the structure is cyclic and the key is unfindable - bail out as not-found, exactly what the sentinel path does.
THE LOG CAP WAS HIDING THE RESULT. With the bound in, kernel_calls read 200 - which is exactly where the `[KERNEL] #%d` trace was capped, and smoke_spread/progress derive kernel_calls by COUNTING those lines. Raised the cap to 4000 and the true figure is 1,426. Anyone measuring against a capped trace measures the cap. Worth watching for again if progress ever parks precisely on a round number.
NOW: crash, not hang, at 1,426 calls in sub_00202B87+0x35E reading MEM32(edx + 0xDC) with edx = 0xCCCC0004. Nothing of ours writes 0xCC fill - it appears only in game code (recomp_0012.c, recomp_0015.c) - so this is the game's own CRT debug fill being read back, i.e. a buffer used before initialisation.
ON THE "STACK ESCAPE" WARNING: triage reports esp leaving the 8 MB stack at kernel call #57 (0x00F7FC14 -> 0x03DAB9FC) and advises fixing that first. I believe it is a FALSE POSITIVE and did not chase it. 0x03DAB9FC sits near the top of the heap, esp decrements cleanly from there (9FC, 9F8, 9F4 ...), and the boot then performs 1,370 further kernel calls of real work; a genuinely corrupt esp would not survive that. The game appears to switch its main thread onto a heap-allocated stack. Not proven - if the next investigation stalls, prove or disprove it rather than assuming either way.
Signals deterministic over 2 runs at 1426/211/11/192. Probes stripped; watchdog RIP capture back behind #if 0; the new guard is in manual_edits.json (139 records, 139/139 verified). Gate is red on failed_icalls (211 vs 4) and needs a deliberate re-baseline decision now that the run crashes rather than hangs.

message: Registry NULL traced into the engine allocator: small-block path sub_0020F860 returns 0; chain intact, not a missing function
note:
Traced the NULL registry allocation two levels deeper. The dispatch chain is entirely intact - this is a state failure inside the engine's own memory manager, not anything missing.
MEASURED, at sub_001EC5E0 (the manager's allocate thunk):
  this=0x00F81288 vtbl=0x003F4770 f_AC=0x0001 target=0x00211530 size=0x00000010
So the thunk reads a valid vtable, resolves vtable+0x1AC to 0x00211530, and dispatches. MEM16(this+0xAC) is 1, not zero - my guess last turn that a zero field at +0xAC was the cause is WRONG.
sub_00211530 is the engine memory manager's allocate - a ~1,600 line function. Traced the path for this request: esi (alignment) starts from the caller's slot, is maxed against MEM16(ebp+0xAC)=1, then forced up to 8 by `if (LO16(esi) < 8) esi = 8`. At loc_00211E1C with ebx == 0 (no existing block to resize) it tests `if (LO16(esi) <= 8)`, which is true, so the request goes to sub_0020F860 - the small-block path - and NOT sub_00210E50. Whatever that returns lands in esi at loc_00211E37, and `if (esi == 0)` falls into the failure reporting at loc_00212058, which is how a 0 gets back to the caller.
PROVENANCE CHECKED, because a fabricated seed extent would explain a bogus body: both sub_0020F860 and sub_00210E50 are genuine `call_target` detections in seeded_functions.json (0x0020F860-0x002106A4 and 0x00210E50-0x00210EA5) living in a generated chunk, not seeder-fabricated. So their bodies are real.
NEXT, and it is now a single question: probe sub_0020F860's return value and, if it is 0, its internal failure branch. That function is the small-block allocator, so the likely candidates are an empty free list or a pool/segment field the manager never populated - note sub_00211530 reads a lot of manager state (+0x18, +0x50..0x5C, +0x68, +0x78, +0x98, +0x9C, +0xB4, +0xB8, +0xBC, +0xC0) and the manager's ctor sub_002154F0 leaves most of it zero, so a zero pool descriptor is plausible. Do not guard the caller - a NULL here is the manager correctly reporting that it has no memory to give, and guarding it would just move the crash.
Also worth recording: I hand-wrote this turn's probe through a shell heredoc and the `\n` in the C format string arrived as a real newline, breaking the build with C2001 - exactly the failure add_probe.py exists to prevent, and documented in its own header. Use the probe tool, or the editor, never a heredoc.

message: ROOT CAUSE: engine memory manager has no memory range (base=0, limits=-1) - allocations return tiny offsets and corrupt low memory
note:
ROOT CAUSE FOUND, and it is one fact that explains the whole cascade: THE ENGINE MEMORY MANAGER HAS NO MEMORY RANGE.
Probed at sub_00211530's small-block path (loc_00211E37), reading the manager through ebp:
  ret=0x00000008  f18(base)=0x00000000  f98=0xFFFFFFFF  f9C=0xFFFFFFFF
  (and from the previous probe: f78=0x00000000  fB4=0x00000000  fC0=0x00000004)
Base is ZERO and the two limit fields are -1, i.e. never set. So sub_0020F860 computes base + offset = 0 + 8 and hands back 8. The allocator is not failing - it is succeeding against an empty range, which is worse, because 8 is non-NULL and every caller believes it.
CORRECTION TO LAST TURN: I recorded that sub_0020F860 "returns 0". It does not - it returns 8. The 0 the registry ends up storing comes from further downstream, not from the allocator itself.
WHAT THIS EXPLAINS, all previously logged as separate mysteries:
- The class registry tables at 0x5BC538/0x5BC53C are 0, because the 0xC-byte allocation that should back them produced a bogus pointer.
- 211 failed indirect calls whose targets are small integers (0x00-0x08, 0x10, 0x16, 0x26, 0x38, 0x44, 0x54, 0x64, 0x6C, 0x70): those are objects allocated at tiny addresses, so their "vtable" is whatever integer sits in low memory.
- The 0xCCCC0004 read: a partially-written low-memory dword being used as a vtable.
- Guest VA 0 containing 0x00F81288 earlier, and the heap lock at heap+0x580 going from 0x00F81610 to 0 - both are LOW MEMORY CORRUPTION. Follow the code after loc_0021202E: with esi=8 and ebx=0 it reaches loc_002120AE and memsets MEM32(esp+0x40) bytes starting at edi=8. That writes straight over the fake TIB at guest 0-0xFF, which is why fs:[0] and fs:[4] changed under us. Those two anomalies were symptoms, not separate bugs - do not chase them again.
NO KERNEL MEMORY QUERY IS INVOLVED. The full ordinal set the boot uses is 24, 47, 107 (KeInitializeDpc), 113 (KeInitializeTimerEx), 128 (KeQuerySystemTime), 149 (KeSetTimer), 184 (NtAllocateVirtualMemory), 187 (NtClose), 202 (NtOpenFile), 218 (NtQueryVolumeInformationFile), 255 (PsCreateSystemThreadEx), 277/291/294 (critical sections), 301 (RtlNtStatusToDosError). There is no MmQueryStatistics or equivalent, so the manager's range is not meant to come from the kernel at all - the engine hands it a block it obtained itself.
STRONGEST HYPOTHESIS, not yet proven: that block cannot be obtained because the CRT heap is tiny. NtAllocateVirtualMemory is called exactly TWICE in the entire boot - a 1 MB MEM_RESERVE (type 0x2000) and a 4 KB MEM_COMMIT (type 0x1000) that the bridge logged as "MEM_COMMIT on existing region, no-op". heap_allocs is 11. An engine asking for a multi-megabyte pool out of a 1 MB reserved / 4 KB committed heap gets nothing, and if that failure is unchecked the manager keeps base = 0.
NEXT: find the call that should write manager+0x18 / +0x98 / +0x9C and probe what it is given. sub_00239E50 publishes the manager then immediately calls sub_00236500(this=manager), which is the natural place for "here is your pool". Watch 0x00F8128 + 0x18 - i.e. the guest VA of manager+0x18 - with run --watch to catch the writer directly; that address is stable across runs. If it is never written, work back to whichever allocation was supposed to supply the block and check whether NtAllocateVirtualMemory should be committing more than 4 KB.
Do NOT paper over this with a guard at the allocator. A manager with base=0 is not a pointer bug, it is missing initialisation, and guarding the symptom moves the crash without recovering the memory.

message: Allocator is debug-instrumented; sub_0020F860 signature corrected; three cheaper questions queued before diving into free-list internals
note:
Two facts learned about the allocator, and a deliberate stop before an open-ended reverse-engineering dive.
1. THE MANAGER IS A DEBUG-INSTRUMENTED ALLOCATOR. sub_00211530 is riddled with guard-band constants - 0xAAAAAAAF and 0xBBBBBBBF as header/footer magic, 0xFDFDFDFD as no-mans-land fill, 0xCDCDCDCD for fresh blocks - and with __debugbreak() on every mismatch, gated behind debug levels in manager+0xB8 and +0xBC. Both of those are 0, so the checking paths are skipped. This matters for interpretation: 0xCCCC0004, which I chased twice as "uninitialised memory", is this allocator's fill vocabulary, not evidence of a translation fault. Read those constants as intentional from now on.
2. sub_0020F860 TAKES AN ARGUMENT, and I nearly mis-read it as taking none. Its body reads MEM32(esp + 0x2C), which after `esp -= 0x1C` plus three pushes is the first argument slot, not a local. The caller supplies it at loc_00211E1C with `PUSH32(esp, eax)` before branching to loc_00211E30, where the call itself passes only ecx = this. So the signature is AllocSmall(this, size) and the size arrives from `eax = edx + edi` computed at loc_00211BE1. Anyone probing this function should print MEM32(esp + 0x2C), not assume a zero-arg thiscall.
WHY THE RANGE CHECK DOES NOT SAVE US: at loc_00211639 the guard is `CMP_B(0, MEM32(ebp + 0x9C))`, and with +0x9C = 0xFFFFFFFF that unsigned compare is trivially true, so control reaches the allocation at loc_00211BE1 regardless of base being 0. The uninitialised limits do not merely fail to protect - they actively wave the request through.
WATCH DID NOT WORK HERE, for the third time: 0x00F812A0 (manager+0x18) fired on the allocator's own zeroing from a system routine and disarmed. run --watch is page-granular and single-shot, so it is only useful for a field that is written ONCE and late. Stop reaching for it on freshly allocated memory.
STOPPING POINT, chosen deliberately. Following the 8 further means reverse-engineering ~1,500 lines of a debug allocator's free-list and segment logic with no hypothesis to test, which is not the cheapest next move. The cheaper questions, in order:
  a) Does this allocation happen before the engine's memory system is initialised at all? sub_00239E50 -> sub_00236500 is static-init-time; if the pool is supposed to be handed over later, then a 0xC-byte request at this point may be expected to come from somewhere else entirely, and the bug is that it is routed here.
  b) Only TWO NtAllocateVirtualMemory calls occur in the whole boot (1 MB reserve, 4 KB commit logged as a no-op) against 11 heap allocs. Whatever the engine intends as its pool, it never asks the kernel for it. Establish whether it should - if a large commit is expected and our bridge is refusing or no-oping it, that is a small fix in our code rather than a large one in theirs.
  c) sub_0020F860's own free-list head lives at manager+0x70 (read into esi at loc_0020F895). If that is 0, the small-block path has no pool and the 8 is an offset from nothing - one probe answers it.
Tree is clean: no probes or temporary traces anywhere, manual_edits verifies 139/139, working tree committed. Signals deterministic at 1426/211/11/192.

message: CORRECTION: the allocator DOES have a valid pool - retracting the no-memory-range headline; open question is why it returns 8
note:
CORRECTING MY OWN "ROOT CAUSE" ENTRY. I recorded that the engine memory manager "has no memory range" on the strength of manager+0x18 being 0 and +0x98/+0x9C being -1. That claim is too strong and the headline should not stand as written.
The falsifying measurement, one probe inside sub_0020F860 at loc_0020F895:
  freelist70=0x00F835C8  size=0x00000010  base18=0x00000000  f74=0x00000001
manager+0x70 is a VALID heap pointer (heap base is 0x00F80000), and the requested size is a correct 0x10. So the small-block allocator does have a pool, and it is being asked for a sane amount. What +0x18 actually feeds is the resize-existing-block path at loc_00211639 (`eax = MEM32(ebp + 0x18) + edi`), not the pool base - so a zero there is not obviously wrong, and I mapped it to "base" without evidence.
WHAT SURVIVES from that entry, and is still measured:
- sub_0020F860 returns 8, and 8 is then used as an absolute pointer (loc_00211E45 does MEM32(esi + -4), i.e. MEM32(4)).
- The range check at loc_00211639 is `CMP_B(0, MEM32(ebp + 0x9C))` with +0x9C = 0xFFFFFFFF, so it waves the request through regardless. Uninitialised limits still fail to protect even if they are not the cause.
- The low-memory corruption chain is unchanged and still explains VA 0 changing, the heap lock at heap+0x580 being zeroed, the 211 small-integer indirect-call targets, and the 0xCCCC read: with esi=8 and ebx=0, control reaches loc_002120AE and memsets from guest address 8 over the fake TIB. Those remain symptoms of the bogus 8, not separate defects.
WHAT IS NOW OPEN: why a free-list allocator with a valid pool head at 0x00F835C8 hands back 8 for a 16-byte request. Candidates, cheapest first: the free list is intact but the returned value is an OFFSET the caller should add to a base (in which case the caller's use of it as an absolute pointer is the translation bug, and that is our fault not the game's); or the list is corrupt and node 8 is garbage; or a size/bucket computation in the 1,512-line body picks a bogus bin. The first is worth testing before the others because it would be a lifter or ABI mistake rather than an RE problem - check whether the original x86 at the return site adds a base to eax.
METHOD NOTE, third occurrence: run --watch is page-granular and single-shot, so on freshly allocated memory it fires on the allocator's own zeroing and disarms. It is only useful for a field written once and late. Stop reaching for it here.
Tree is clean - no probes or traces, manual_edits 139/139, signals deterministic at 1426/211/11/192 over 2 runs.

message: Seeded 13 static-init functions: crash gone, 1426 -> 1456 calls; now a 612M-dispatch spin on a heap address
note:
Seeded 13 more missing functions. The access violation is GONE, kernel_calls 1426 -> 1456, failed indirect calls 211 -> 199. The run now ends in a spin instead of a crash.
HOW THEY WERE FOUND, and this is the reusable bit: whatis.py over every unresolved ICALL target that lands in .text and is absent from seeded_functions.json. 81 candidates; 65 disassembled to something. Thirteen of those share one unmistakable signature -
    mov al, byte ptr [<flag>] / test al,al / jne skip / push <descriptor> / mov byte [<flag>],1 / call 0x209650
- which is the C++ run-once static-initialiser guard, and 0x209650 is the class-registration runner. Those are certainly real function entries: 0x001A7600, 0x002370B0, 0x00246030, 0x00246090, 0x002460F0, 0x00246150, 0x00246560, 0x002471B0, 0x0027B1D0, 0x0027B9B0, 0x00285DB0, 0x002895A0, 0x00304010. seed_list 1,071 -> 1,084.
The remaining 52 were deliberately NOT seeded and should not be: they decode as `into`, `pop ss`, `push cs`, `int3`, `add byte ptr [eax], al` (a run of 00 bytes), `sbb`, `ror`, `xchg`, `cdq`, `div`, and page-aligned round numbers like 0x11000 / 0x40000 / 0x100000 / 0x140000 / 0x382000-0x38F000. Those are mid-instruction garbage and data misread as pointers - the log already records that adding junk seeds made things worse before. If more are wanted, the filter is "first instruction is a plausible function prologue", not "lands in .text".
WHAT safe_stub 192 -> ~9,000 ACTUALLY MEANS, because it looks alarming and is not what it appears: sub_00ICALL_SAFE_STUB is rate-limited to the first 8 hits then every 65,536, so ~9,000 log lines is about 600 MILLION real stub calls. Confirmed independently: the watchdog reports 612,707,524 dispatches. And the run-to-run variation (8,646 / 8,910 / 9,146) is NOT nondeterministic behaviour - the watchdog kills the process after a fixed 8 s, so each run simply gets a different distance through the same spin. Do not read that VARIES flag as a real signal here.
THE SPIN: every one of the last 16 ICALL targets is 0x030FEFE8, a HEAP address being called as a function. So an object's function-pointer field holds a data address. The watchdog RIP landed inside a system DLL (we were in fprintf at the sample instant) but the stack resolved to recomp_icall_fail_log, sub_0019B870+0x67 and sub_002235D0+0xF31 - so it is still inside the class registrar. sub_0019B870 itself is three instructions and no loop, so the sample merely caught it there; the loop is above it in sub_002235D0.
Also ruled out: our own logging is not the bottleneck. Both the SAFE_STUB path and recomp_icall_fail_log are rate-limited, and 600M dispatches in 8 s is about 75M/s, which is a tight loop doing almost nothing, not I/O.
HONEST ASSESSMENT of whether this is better: kernel_calls and failed_icalls both improved and the crash is gone, but a spin replaced it, so this is not unambiguously forward. The next step is to find the loop in sub_002235D0 that keeps calling 0x030FEFE8, using the watchdog RIP capture (main.c, #if 0) which is the only instrument that has worked on a quiet loop.
Snapshot taken. manual_edits 139/139. Gate will flag both the safe_stub rise and the nondeterminism; both are explained above and neither should be baselined away.

message: Allocator: free list legitimately empty, frame bridge OK, rebase theory dead - the 8 comes via sub_0020F209's early exit to sub_0020F0B2
note:
Two more levels of the allocator, TWO MORE HYPOTHESES KILLED, and a precise handover point. No signal change - this entry is worth reading for what it rules out.
MEASURED THIS ROUND:
1. The free list is EMPTY, and legitimately so. At sub_0020EFD0's branch the cursor MEM32(pool+0x2C) = 0x00F83610 and the head sentinel pool+0x48 = 0x00F835C8 + 0x48 = 0x00F83610. They are equal, which is exactly how an initialised-but-empty circular list looks. So control takes the else branch at loc_0020F0FD into sub_0020F209 - the "no free block, carve a new one" path. Nothing is corrupt here; the allocator is behaving correctly for an empty list.
2. HYPOTHESIS DEAD - the fragment's frame is NOT clobbered. sub_0020F209 is an fpo_leaf fragment that inherits ebp through the g_seh_ebp global, which the notes flag as fragile, so I expected a bad inherited frame. Probed at its entry: ebp=0x00F83610, esi=0x00F81288 (the manager), g_seh_ebp=0x00F83610. All three correct. The frame bridge is working. Do not re-chase this.
3. HYPOTHESIS DEAD - the return value is not a mis-rebased offset. Every success path in sub_0020F209 computes `eax = (MEM32(block) >> 31 << 3 | 4) + block`, i.e. block_base + 4 or + 12. With ebp = 0x00F83610 that yields 0x00F83614 or 0x00F8361C. For the observed 8 the base would have to be 4, and it is not. Combined with the earlier finding that three of sub_0020F860's six return paths rebase their own result, "the caller forgot to add a base" is now doubly dead.
WHERE THE 8 MUST COME FROM: sub_0020F209 has early exits at loc_0020F480, loc_0020F491 and loc_0020F4A7 that tail-call sub_0020F0B2() and return ITS value, bypassing the block-base arithmetic entirely. That is the only route by which a value unrelated to 0x00F836xx can reach the caller. sub_0020F0B2 is the next thing to read, and it is level seven of this chain.
FULL CHAIN AS IT STANDS, every link measured:
  sub_001F6FB0 -> sub_001EC5E0 -> sub_00211530 -> sub_0020F860 (return path 5)
    -> sub_0020EFD0 -> sub_0020F209 -> sub_0020F0B2 [NEXT]
Cheapest next step: probe sub_0020F0B2's entry and its return value, plus which of the three early exits was taken (the guards are sub_001E8F30 returning nonzero, twice, then an ICALL through vtable+0x54 returning nonzero). Those three are "grow the pool" attempts - so the likely story is that growing FAILS and the failure value propagates out as 8, which would make the real question "why can this allocator not grow its pool", not "why is the arithmetic wrong".
That reframing matters: nothing in five levels of arithmetic has been wrong. Every value checked has been correct for its context. The defect is looking more like a failed pool growth than a corrupted pointer, and pool growth is where the engine would ask the CRT - or the kernel - for more memory. Recall that NtAllocateVirtualMemory is called exactly twice in the whole boot (1 MB reserve, 4 KB commit logged as a no-op).

message: TIB moved off guest 0 to 0x00770000: did NOT fix the spin, cost 4 calls, kept for correctness
note:
MOVED THE TIB OFF GUEST ADDRESS 0. It did NOT fix the spin, and it cost 4 kernel calls. Both facts up front, because I predicted otherwise.
WHAT I GOT WRONG. I found that sub_001E8F30 - the engine's "ask every handler to free memory" pass - reads its handler count as `eax = MEM32(0x5BC53C); edi = MEM32(eax + 4)`, and with that registry pointer NULL the count came from MEM32(4), which was the TIB's TLS-array slot holding 0x00750000. A 7.6-million-iteration loop over garbage, and I concluded that was the 600M-dispatch spin. It is a real hazard and the arithmetic is right, but it is NOT the spin: the spin-probe backtrace - which I already had - names sub_001F7930, and it is unchanged after the move. I reasoned from a mechanism I had just discovered instead of from the evidence already in hand. The backtrace was right the first time.
THE CHANGE ITSELF IS STILL SOUND, and I am keeping it. The TIB now lives at XBOX_TIB_VA 0x00770000 with g_fs_base pointing at it, and guest 0x0-0xFF is left zero. It sat at 0 only because the lifter used to drop fs: prefixes so fs:[n] became MEM32(n); that stopped being true when fs: lifting landed (2,743 sites now use g_fs_base). Leaving it at 0 meant the TIB also answered every NULL-DERIVED READ, so a null pointer silently yielded plausible-looking data instead of zero. That property is exactly what misled me above, and it will mislead the next investigation too. The self pointer at +0x18 is now a real address rather than the 0 it was forced to be.
COST: kernel_calls 1456 -> 1452, deterministic. Five absolute low-memory reads remain in the whole generated tree - MEM32(0xC) twice, MEM32(0x54), MEM32(0x1C), MEM32(0x14) - so fs: lifting is essentially complete and those five are the likely source of the loss. They are either genuine DS reads of Xbox low memory or the last unlifted fs: sites; establishing which is a bounded job and the obvious follow-up. I am NOT claiming the four calls are unimportant, only that the trade buys a memory model where a null read reads null, which is a prerequisite for both per-thread TIBs and for trusting any future null-pointer diagnosis.
WHY NOT REVERT: this session already removed one change that did nothing (the widened bootstrap gate, proven redundant by identical signals). This one is different - it changes behaviour, it is architecturally required for the per-thread TIB work, and its cost is traceable to five identified sites rather than being a mystery. If those five turn out to want real TIB values, the fix is to lift them, not to move the TIB back.
THE SPIN IS UNCHANGED and still the open item: sub_001F7930 iterating count = MEM32(MEM32(this+0x28) + 0xC) with a virtual call per entry, reached via sub_00011E40 -> sub_00239E50 -> sub_00209650 -> sub_002282E0 -> sub_00209650 -> sub_00227F50 -> sub_002235D0. Note this+0x28 is NOT null - if it were, MEM32(0 + 0xC) would now read zero from the cleared low memory and the loop would be skipped. So that object pointer is a garbage non-null value, which is consistent with it having come from the allocator that returns 8.
Signals: 1452/198/11/~9700, hang, deterministic apart from the time-boxed safe_stub count.

message: sub_0020F0B2 is the retry-loop head; the bogus 8 never escapes - sub_00211530 converts it to an honest failure
note:
Read sub_0020F0B2 from the recorded chain rather than re-deriving it, and it closes the loop on the allocator's SHAPE - though not yet on the cause.
sub_0020F0B2 IS THE RETRY-LOOP HEAD, not a leaf. Its body is character-for-character the same logic as loc_0020F0AC inside sub_0020EFD0: re-read the cursor MEM32(pool+0x2C), recompute the block size, compare against the head sentinel pool+0x48, then dispatch to sub_0020F10A when they differ or tail-jump to sub_0020F209 when they match. So the allocator's structure is a CYCLE, not a chain:
    sub_0020EFD0 -> sub_0020F209 -> (a handler freed something?) -> sub_0020F0B2 -> sub_0020F209 ...
sub_0020F209's three early exits at loc_0020F480 / loc_0020F491 / loc_0020F4A7 are all "memory was reclaimed, go round again", guarded by two sub_001E8F30 calls and an ICALL through vtable+0x54. That is why the chain looked endless: I was walking a loop and expecting a bottom.
TWO MEASUREMENTS THAT DISAGREE, and the disagreement is the useful part:
    sub_0020F860 path 5 returns 0x00000008
    sub_001F6FB0, the registry caller, receives 0x00000000
So the bogus 8 does NOT escape. sub_00211530 sits between them and converts it into an honest failure - its return is MEM32(esp + 0x3C), which the failure paths set to 0. The registry is therefore being told the truth: the allocation failed. That kills any idea that a corrupted pointer is being handed out and used; the outer layer is behaving correctly and the tables are NULL because the allocation genuinely could not be served.
This reframes the whole investigation for the third time, and each reframe has been narrower. Not "the arithmetic is wrong" (five levels of correct arithmetic), not "a bad pointer leaks out" (it does not), but simply: A 16-BYTE ALLOCATION CANNOT BE SERVED FROM A POOL THAT HAS A VALID HEAD AT 0x00F835C8 AND AN EMPTY FREE LIST. The pool exists, the free list is legitimately empty, growth is attempted, growth reports nothing gained, and the request fails.
The remaining question is therefore about the POOL'S EXTENT, not its pointers: whether it was ever given a region to carve from. Concrete fields to read, all off esi (the manager) inside sub_0020F209: +0xA8 (tested for zero, gates the whole size-check block), +0x88/+0x8C (a 64-bit running total), +0xC8 (a size), +0x38, +0xB4. And off the pool at MEM32(manager+0x70): +0x2C (cursor), +0x48 (sentinel), +0x7DC. One probe printing those answers whether the pool has any capacity at all.
Worth holding alongside: NtAllocateVirtualMemory is called exactly TWICE in the whole boot - a 1 MB MEM_RESERVE and a 4 KB MEM_COMMIT the bridge logs as a no-op - and xbox_HeapAlloc is the only thing behind it. An engine pool that was never funded would look exactly like this.

message: probe_struct.py added; pool has 1.25MB free and 0 used - the refusal is explicit, traced to sub_001F09D0 vtable+0x6C
note:
NEW TOOL probe_struct.py, and it paid for itself on first use.
"What is in this object right now" is the commonest question in a static recompile, and answering it has cost ONE BUILD-AND-RUN PER FIELD. Today the allocator was probed across roughly eight separate cycles - manager +0x18, +0x30, +0x70, +0x74, +0x98, +0x9C, +0xAC, +0xB4, +0xC0 - several of them only to learn the field was fine. probe_struct.py dumps a whole field set in one probe:
    py -3 tools_data/probe_struct.py recomp_0015.c --after "loc_0020F209: ;" \
        --tag pool --base esi --offsets 0xA8:limit,0xC8:blocksz,0x88:total
It is a THIN WRAPPER over add_probe.py, not a second implementation - add_probe owns the escaping and the /* PROBE */ markers strip_probes.py depends on, and duplicating either would be a second thing to keep correct. --base takes any C expression, so `--base "MEM32(esi + 0x70)"` dumps the object one dereference away. It prints the base itself first, so a null object is visible instead of being inferred from a row of zeroes. Nothing in it is title-specific.
WHAT IT FOUND, in one run instead of six:
    base=0x00F81288 f38=0 total_lo=0 total_hi=0 limit=0x00140000 quantum=0 blocksz=0x10
THE POOL IS NOT STARVED. It has a 1.25 MB limit (0x140000) and has consumed ZERO of it, for a 16-byte request. So every "the pool was never funded" theory - including my own from two entries ago - is wrong. Capacity is available and the size check passes.
THE REFUSAL IS EXPLICIT, not an accident. Following the "fits" path leads to ICALL(vtable + 0x1B0) = sub_001EC9C0, which is the manager asking the system for memory. Measured: it returns 0xFFFFFFFF. Its body is four instructions - if MEM32(this+0xA0) | MEM32(this+0xA4) is non-zero it refuses outright - but both are ZERO, so it takes sub_001EC9D8 instead, which dispatches through a global system-allocator object at 0x5BB9AC (obj=0x0046A72C vtbl=0x003EECB0) to sub_001F09D0. That is where the -1 is born.
WHERE I STOPPED, and the exact next probe: sub_001F09D0's first branch at loc_001F09E0 tests ebx = MEM32(esp + 0x1C). If zero it calls vtable+0x70 = sub_001FE850, which is the RAM-boundary probe the notes warn about - it compares MEM32(0x46A668) >> 26 against MEM32(0x5BBAD0) >> 26, i.e. which 64 MB region the position and the limit fall in. I probed sub_001FE850 and it NEVER FIRES, so ebx is non-zero and control goes to loc_001F0A0D and vtable+0x6C instead. Probe ebx at loc_001F09E0 and follow vtable+0x6C; that is one run from the answer.
FULL CHAIN, every link measured, none inferred:
  sub_001F6FB0 -> sub_001EC5E0 -> sub_00211530 -> sub_0020F860(path5) ->
  sub_0020EFD0 -> sub_0020F209 -> [ICALL vtbl+0x1B0] sub_001EC9C0 ->
  sub_001EC9D8 -> [global 0x5BB9AC] sub_001F09D0 -> [vtbl+0x6C, NEXT]
Also worth keeping: sub_0020F0B2 is the retry-loop HEAD, so this allocator is a cycle rather than a chain - that is why the descent felt bottomless.

message: Seeded 13 tool-recommended fragments: 1452 -> 56, reverted immediately; tool now separates FRAGMENT from LIKELY
note:
I CAUSED A 25x REGRESSION WITH MY OWN TOOL, reverted it inside one cycle, and fixed the tool so it cannot repeat. Negative result, worth more than the attempt was.
WHAT HAPPENED: find_icall_gaps.py offered 15 LIKELY candidates. I dropped the two it flagged as page-aligned and seeded the other 13. Result: kernel_calls 1452 -> 56, heap_allocs 11 -> 6, and a crash returned. Restored seed_list.json from the pre-change copy, re-seeded, rebuilt, confirmed 1452/198/11 back. Total cost one build-and-run each way, because the list was backed up before touching it - do that every time.
THE TOOL'S MISTAKE, and it was mine in the design: it conflated two different questions. The instruction-boundary test proves an address IS a real instruction start. It says nothing about whether SEEDING it is safe. Ten of the thirteen were mid-function jump targets, and seeding one of those emits a FRAGMENT running from that address to the owner's end - duplicating the owner's tail and inheriting a half-built frame. That is sometimes exactly the right fix (it is how the 195 skipped addresses were repaired earlier today) and sometimes it wrecks the boot, and nothing in the disassembly distinguishes the two cases.
FIXED: mid-function boundary hits now classify as FRAGMENT, a separate bucket that --add will NOT touch. They are still reported, with the reason, because they remain real targets worth trying. Adding one requires --add-fragment 0xADDR explicitly, and the tool refuses an address that is not in the current report's fragment list. The self-check that asserted the old LIKELY verdict has been rewritten to assert FRAGMENT and to explain why, plus a new case that fails if a boundary hit ever comes back as LIKELY again. LIKELY dropped from 15 to 4 on the current log.
THE GENERAL LESSON, which applies to any static recomp: "this address is real" and "seeding this address is safe" are independent. A tool that automates the first must not imply the second. Batch-adding anything whose failure mode is unknown is how a 25x regression happens in one step; the fix is per-item addition with a measurement between, which is what --add-fragment now enforces.
Also note the four remaining LIKELY are weak - two are page-aligned round numbers the tool itself flags (0x00011000, 0x0034B000) and the other two are bare `push` openers. There is no cheap win sitting in this list. That is useful to know: the missing-function seam, which paid out three times today, appears to be exhausted for now.
Rule #14 was already triggered before this attempt and remains triggered. Signals restored and unchanged: 1452/198/11, hang, deterministic apart from the time-boxed safe_stub.

message: Replace the CRT RtlAllocateHeap (sub_001A0B0C) with the native heap: 1452 -> 4000 kernel calls, failed icalls 152 -> 2
note: BIGGEST SINGLE MOVE SO FAR, and it is a PORT FIX not scaffolding. Counted first (ledger #28): all 690 allocation failures came from sub_001A02B7, the heap's own free-block finder, returning 0. Two other failure routes in sub_001A0B0C fired ZERO times - notably the kernel call, so the allocator never asked the OS for memory and a bigger pool could not have helped. Replaced the whole function with xbox_HeapAlloc (~55MB native heap vs the 1.25MB pool it was choking on). Result on 2 of 2 runs, deterministic: kernel_calls 1452 -> 4000, failed_icalls 152 -> 2, heap_allocs 11 -> 13, safe_stub 192 -> 8, distinct kernel fns 15 -> 16. Allocator ring now reads 7 allocations, 0 failed, 0 duplicates - previously 697 / 690 / 3. The 697 was the retry loop spinning on failures. This also settles ledger #22: the duplicate returns (0x00F81288 handed out 4x) are gone, so the registry corruption and the sub_001F7930 spin should both be downstream-fixed. NEW WALL: crash at RVA 0xE4259B writing 0xF688BE15 - further along, and exactly the risk called out in the override comment (blocks carry no NT block header, so anything stepping back 8 bytes to read one finds nothing). Memory is never reclaimed - xbox_HeapAlloc only bumps - so RtlFreeHeap is now a leak. Fine for reaching a menu; not fine forever.

message: Implement NtQueryVirtualMemory (ordinal 217) and fix its arg count 16 -> 8: crash gone, stack escape gone, failed icalls 2 -> 1
note: TWO BUGS IN ONE ORDINAL, and it was 3,966 of 4,000 kernel calls. (1) NO BRIDGE AT ALL - it hit the "no bridge, returning 0" fallback, leaving the caller's output buffer untouched so the caller re-read stale data and called again forever. (2) WRONG ARG COUNT - g_slot_arg_bytes said 16 (4 args, the Windows NT signature that docs/formats/kernel-exports.md also documents) but the game pushes 8 (2 args, the real Xbox signature). The bridge pops g_slot_arg_bytes after each call, so it over-popped 8 bytes every time. Measured directly: kernel #108..#113 walk esp 0x00F7FFDC -> 0x00F80004 in exact +8 steps, and after ~4,000 calls esp had climbed clean off the top of the 8MB stack. That is the STACK ESCAPE triage_crash reports, and every register being garbage at the old crash was downstream of it. RESULT, deterministic 2 of 2: crash GONE (was an access violation in sub_0020F209), esp at call #4000 is 0x00F7FDA4 - healthy, inside the stack, where it started. failed_icalls 152 -> 2 -> 1, safe_stub 192 -> 8 -> 1. kernel_calls stays 4000. NOTE THE DOC IS WRONG: docs/formats/kernel-exports.md line 26 lists the 4-parameter NT form for ordinal 217; the Xbox kernel takes (BaseAddress, MemoryInformation) only. Measurement beat the doc (rule #5) and the doc still needs correcting. NEW WALL: a HANG, not a crash - 23.2M dispatches, and the last 16 ICALL targets are all thunk slot 73, so the caller is still walking memory via NtQueryVirtualMemory and not terminating. My bridge reports a fixed 64KB RegionSize for every query, which likely makes a region walk take far more steps than it should; reporting real contiguous extents is the obvious next move.

message: Pool growth fixed: report the heap's free tail as MEM_FREE in NtQueryVirtualMemory

message: Fix deferred-flag miscompile at 0x001F0AB2: region registrar now runs, reached 37 -> 43
note: faithful.py named it exactly: "cmp ecx, eax then mov ecx, esi" at 0x001F0AB2. The lifter dropped the cmp to a no-op and re-tested at the jcc, after `mov ecx, esi` had clobbered ecx - so it compared the object pointer against the SUCCESS code (0x5BC5D8 == 0) instead of the returned status. The branch never fired, so vtable+0x68 (sub_001FE670, the region registrar) never ran, the min/max pair 0x46A668/0x5BBAD0 stayed at identity values (0xFFFFFFFF / 0), and sub_001FE850's "has any region been registered?" gate returned -1 for every allocation. Fix evaluates the compare into a local before the clobber. Deterministic 3/3: reached 37 -> 43 (best ever), heap allocs 9 -> 10 with 0 failed, crash moved sub_001E8F30 -> sub_00205170. The registry allocation at sub_001F6FB0 now takes its SUCCESS path, so the NULL 0x5BC53C registry is fixed downstream. Persisted via manual_edits.py extract. Earlier deepdive reported faithful CLEAN on this function only because it ran with no_faithful=true.

message: Seed sub_001E6C5B and sub_001E6CC9: generic g_esp+=4 stubs were leaking 12 bytes per loop, reached 43 -> 47
note: sub_00205170's deferred-free array was healthy (9 entries, valid blocks). The fault was that its cursor and end live in stack slots MEM32(esp+0x14)/MEM32(esp+0x20) while esp drifted 12 bytes per iteration underneath them - measured 0x00F7FE3C -> FE30 -> FE24 -> FE18. Source: sub_001E6C10 pushes esi+edi then tail-jumps out; its real exits restore 16 bytes, but sub_001E6C5B and sub_001E6CC9 were both generic stubs restoring 4. Seeded both via seed_missing_functions.py --va (purely additive, no regeneration). Each needed its recomp_stubs_unresolved.c line replaced with the "moved to src/recomp_seed.c" marker or LNK2005. Measured one at a time: sub_001E6C5B alone changed nothing (kept anyway - strictly more faithful, not a regression); sub_001E6CC9 is the one - reached 43 -> 47, heap allocs 20 -> 21, and the crash changes category from access violation to integer divide-by-zero, so the coalescer now completes. LESSON: a generic stub is NOT neutral. g_esp += 4 is only right for a plain ret with no callee-saved pushes; otherwise it corrupts the caller's frame and surfaces far away. Sweep recomp_stubs_unresolved.c for stubs that are tail-jump targets of functions with pushes. New wall: divide-by-zero at sub_001FAB40+0x83D, ecx=edx=0.

message: Session summary: PAST the original sub_001F7930 wall - 677M dispatches to 188, reached 33 -> 47
note: Position vs the ORIGINAL wall, since that is the question worth answering periodically. Then: indirect-call dispatches 677,120,348, failed icalls 199, safe stubs 192, allocations 697 tried / 690 failed, run ended in a spin that never finished. STRATEGIC NOTE: all five fixes today were instances of three CLASSES, not one-offs - (1) deferred-flag miscompiles, which faithful.py detects by name and can SWEEP; (2) generic `g_esp += 4` stubs in recomp_stubs_unresolved.c, wrong for any function with callee-saved pushes; (3) the g_seh_ebp publish gap - ebp is the only register modelled as a per-function local, published on 563 tail-jumps and 0 of 1624 ABI_CALL sites. Classes 1 and 2 each produced a measurable reached gain from a SINGLE instance. Sweeping class 1 is one command and already exists. Recommend running it before crawling another wall.

message: Seed sub_001F840B: jump-table targets were unregistered so every RECOMP_ITAIL failed, reached 47 -> 54
note: Traced an 8-byte esp leak from sub_001FAB40 down through the printf path. sub_001F8350, sub_001EB390 and sub_001EB3AC are all BALANCED (probed every boundary; __chkstk in sub_00341D40 is modelled correctly, -0x1000 exactly). The loss is entirely at the ICALL through the output hook at 0x46A3BC, which holds sub_001F83D0. That function pushes esi, loads a switch index, and dispatches via RECOMP_ITAIL(MEM32(esi*4 + 0x1F84AC)); its balanced exit does POP esi. Measured: entry esp=0x00F7ED70 esi=0x011CD000, idx=4, target 0x001F840B - and the balanced exit fires ZERO times. The tail jump never lands, so the POP never runs: 4 bytes leak and the caller gets esi = 0x00000004, the switch index, which for two turns looked like a plausible object pointer. ROOT CAUSE: none of the 7 jump-table entries at 0x001F84AC is defined or present in recomp_dispatch.c. The lifter emitted the switch cases as unreachable blocks inside sub_001F83D0 but never registered them, so every ITAIL through the table fails. Seeded 0x001F840B (the index actually taken): reached 47 -> 54, kernel_calls 65 -> 82, heap_allocs 21 -> 22, crash changes from divide-by-zero to an access violation at VA 0xFFFFFFFD in sub_00205170+0x6F3. The other four unregistered entries (0x001F83EF/F6/FD, 0x001F8404) will fail identically when their index comes up. SWEEPABLE: any RECOMP_ITAIL whose jump-table targets are absent from recomp_dispatch.c has this bug - a mechanical check over the whole tree.

message: RTTI class recovery: 2,849 functions named from MSVC RTTI, 334 seed candidates found; first seed (sub_0013F920, IAlchemyObjectPool) is neutral
note:
NEW TOOL tools/ghidra_naming/rtti_names.py. The XBE was compiled with RTTI enabled and the project had never used it: Ghidra's program carried 41 non-default symbols and all 26,506 recomp functions were sub_XXXXXXXX. Ghidra cannot do this itself - its MSVC RTTI analyzer is PE-specific and list-analyzers offers none for an XBE - so the tool parses the file directly, walking TypeDescriptor -> CompleteObjectLocator -> vtable[-1].

RECOVERED from XML1: 873 type descriptors, 743 validated COLs (954 candidates rejected), 743 vtables, 726 distinct classes, 2,849 functions named ClassName__vfN. Correctness signal: 82% of named functions land on addresses seeded_functions.json already knows are function starts, which a broken address walk could not do.

A REAL BUG I SHIPPED AND THEN CAUGHT, worth recording because the failure mode is not obvious. The first run used "is this section executable?" as the code test. The XBE marks EVERY section executable except the two $$X image blobs - including .rdata and .data. So the vtable walk ran off the end of each table into read-only data. Consequences: method counts were inflated (CBlock read 41 slots against the sequel's 1, which is what exposed it), 2,147 functions were wrongly flagged ambiguous, and 454 of 791 "missing function" candidates were data pointers rather than code - 57 percent of the list. Fixed by deciding code membership from section NAME (CODE_SECTIONS = .text plus the linked XDK libraries). After the fix: named 1,731 -> 2,849, ambiguous 2,147 -> 574, candidates 791 -> 336. GENERAL LESSON for anything reading XBE section flags: the executable bit does not distinguish code from data in this format, so do not use it as one.

SEED CANDIDATES: 336 addresses are vtable slot targets that seeded_functions.json does not know are functions. Only 2 are mid-function (fragment risk), so 334 are clean. This is stronger evidence than the icall-failure lists used before, because a vtable entry is a fact the compiler emitted rather than an inference drawn from a failure. Written to tools_data/rtti_missing_functions.json with the owning class for each.

FIRST SEED IS NEUTRAL. Picked sub_0013F920 (IAlchemyObjectPool) as the most boot-relevant of the 17 memory-class candidates. Deterministic 2 of 2 after seeding: 44 kernel calls, 5 failed icalls, 23 heap allocs, 8 safe stubs, reached 101 - every signal identical to before. Kept anyway on the sub_001E6C5B precedent: strictly more faithful, measurably not a regression. seed_list.json was backed up to seed_list.json.bak-rtti first.

STRATEGIC FINDING THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE SEED, and it should stop anyone grinding this list blind. The current run's five failed indirect calls are 0x1, 0x0, 0x10, 0xFFFFFFFF and 0xB - small integers and -1, not addresses. So NOTHING in this boot is currently calling a missing function and failing. The wall is a NULL-derived write inside already-lifted code at sub_00204800+0x24D, not an absent function. Seeding all 334 one at a time would cost roughly 22 hours of build-and-run to fix a class of defect that is not what is currently stopping the boot. The candidates are real and worth keeping; they are simply not the bottleneck. Revisit them after the sub_00204800 wall falls, when the boot reaches code that actually dispatches through these vtables.

RTTI ALSO SETTLED THE XML2 DIFF QUESTION, and the answer is narrower than hoped. Running the same tool over XML2's XBE: 1,057 descriptors, 899 vtables, 881 classes. 549 classes are shared with XML1, but only 329 (59.9%) have identical vtable shapes, and every memory class differs by exactly one method - CMemory 12 vs 13, CMemory::IMemoryPoolInfo 9 vs 10, IAlchemyObjectPool 2 vs 3, CEntityAllocator 5 vs 6. A uniform +1 is what a shared base class gaining one virtual looks like. So class names transfer between the two games, but slot-by-slot method transfer does not.

message: Ticket 02 / ledger #82-#83: re-applied the sub_00204020 _icall_esp fix and measured callsites alongside reached, then probed the crash it exposes. H1 dead (reached 101->64 AND callsites 357->265, kernel_calls flat, 37 lost / 0 gained), but the fix is mechanically correct - esp escape gone, sub_0021ACD0's loop stops drifting. Probed ebp at loc_0021AD62/loc_0021AD68: HEALTHY (0x011D6000, 0x011D7000), so #82's refcount lead is refuted. Real fault is MEM32(edi - 4) at recomp_0016.c:2886 with edi = MEM32(esi + 0xC) and esi = 1; esi is already 0 on the surviving iterations, so sub_0021ACD0 walks a NULL object throughout and only guest VA 0 being mapped hides it. Fix and probes reverted; tree unchanged at baseline.

Ticket 02 / ledger #84: full chain traced for the crash the sub_00204020 fix exposes. sub_0021ACD0 is entered ONCE with a GOOD this (0x01091AB0) - all three passes are loop iterations, correcting #83's guess of a second invocation. PRIMARY DEFECT: the container is empty at the indices read - MEM32(this+0x28)=0x01096B88, its +8 is the array 0x010906F0, and elements at +8 and +0xC are both NULL while the count exceeds the start index 2. With esi=0 the code reads AND WRITES guest VA 0xC (mapped, so no fault); iteration 1 stores there, iteration 2 reads it back as a live object and runs the destructor path at loc_0021AD72. THAT PATH LEAKS 16 BYTES - loop-head esp 00F7FDAC, 00F7FDAC, 00F7FD9C - so loc_0021AD20 reloads esi/ebx/ebp from the wrong stack slots and esi comes back as 2. Fourth instance of the #46 pattern. So the sub_00204020 fix is necessary but NOT sufficient: it removes the 8-byte drift and a second, independent 16-byte leak survives it. Next: who populates 0x010906F0, via run(watch="0x010906F8:4:elem2"). Fix and probes reverted; tree unchanged at baseline.

Ticket 02 / ledger #85: write-watch run on the sub_0021ACD0 container. PROVEN - the guest VA 0xC scribble comes from our own lifted code, RVA 0xF41BDD = sub_0021ACD0 + 0x52D = loc_0021ADB4 (`MEM32(esi + 0xC) = ebp` at recomp_0016.c:2927), confirming #84's prediction by measurement. TOOLING LIMIT FOUND, and it is the more reusable result: the watch is ONE-SHOT and PAGE-GRANULAR, so on both the element array (0x010906F8) and the container count (0x01096B94) it caught our own heap zero-fill from a system-DLL memset at RIP 0x7FFAD2EAE579 (outside our module) and then went blind. The arrayptr watch never firing is NOT evidence nobody wrote it - #84's probes read 0x010906F0 out of that slot, so the page protection was simply already gone. RULE: a write-watch cannot answer "who initialised this heap field", only "who corrupted this already-live page". Still open: why the count at MEM32(0x01096B88 + 0xC) exceeds 2 while elements at +8 and +0xC of 0x010906F0 are NULL. Next and now cheap thanks to the RTTI work: read the vtable at MEM32(0x01096B88), look it up in tools/ghidra_naming/rtti_names.json for the class name, then probe that class's element-add method. Fix reverted; tree unchanged at baseline 44/5/23/8, reached 101, callsites 357.

Root cause of the sub_00204800 wall traced end to end: the allocator-owner lookup sub_001E8E20 returns NULL for a live buffer, the caller dereferences it unchecked, and because guest VA 0 is mapped the block-size query silently answers 0 - so every array grow wipes the whole array instead of just its new tail.
note: 2026-08-08, ledger #86-#88. No behaviour change - this is a diagnosis, so the zero delta is expected. FULL CHAIN, every link probed rather than reasoned, all deterministic at 44/5/23/8. sub_00221F50 reads a container's count as a START INDEX then calls sub_00209470 to add N elements. sub_00209470 calls a factory per element (measured returning REAL objects every time - 0x010902A0, 0x010902D8, 0x01090310 ... - so "the factory returns NULL" is refuted) and stores each at MEM32(buffer + count*4). A trace-mode watch on the count field showed it climbing 1,2,3...0x16 from sub_00209470+0x7C2, so 27 elements really were added; the count is honest. Yet the container ends with count 27, a 4-slot buffer and ALL SLOTS NULL. WHY: sub_00202B87 (the array grow) asks the allocator how big the current block is via ICALL vtable+0x144, shifts right 2 for a capacity, remembers that as the OLD capacity, and after growing zeroes only from old-capacity onward. The query returns 0 on all ten grows, so old capacity reads 0 and the zero-run starts at slot 0, wiping every live element - the trace shows exactly one survivor each time (#3 s1, #4 s2, #5 s3) with element 2 erased IN PLACE while the buffer did not move, which is what ruled out "the realloc fails to copy". Capacity 0 also makes sub_00209470's `if (count < capacity) skip grow` never true, so it grows on EVERY add - 12 grows for 27 adds, a second symptom of the same cause. AND WHY THE QUERY RETURNS 0: it is never actually called. sub_001E8E20 ("which allocator owns this pointer?") walks registries 0x5BC53C then 0x5BC538 asking each entry vtable+0x148 "is this yours?", and returns NULL when nothing claims it. sub_00202B87 does not check, so `edx = MEM32(0)` reads guest VA 0 - WHICH IS MAPPED - yielding 0 instead of faulting; the icall target becomes 0, the call fails, and eax stays 0. Measured owner=0 on all ten grows. That also accounts for the failed-icall target 0x00000000 in the run's list. STILL OPEN, and now the sharp question: why does no registered allocator claim a buffer that an allocator in that same registry handed out? The constructor sub_00202C70 allocates it through registry 0x5BC538 via vtable+0xCC. Next probe is inside sub_001E8E20 - print the entry count MEM32(reg+4) for both registries and the per-entry vtable+0x78 / vtable+0x148 results, to see whether the walk runs zero times or runs and is answered false. Note 0x5BC538/0x5BC53C are the same registry pair ledger #36/#43/#44 found NULL and repaired, so verify they are fully POPULATED now, not merely non-NULL. ALSO SETTLED: the container class has NO RTTI (its vtable 0x003EEF28 has a zero COL pointer at vtable[-1]), so ledger #85's "look the class name up in rtti_names.json" is a dead end - recorded as #86 so it is not retried. SYSTEMIC FINDING WORTH ITS OWN TICKET: mapping guest VA 0 is hiding null-pointer dereferences across the whole port - both this bug and the VA 0xC read/write in #84/#85 stayed silent only because page 0 is readable and writable. An opt-in debug build leaving guest page 0 unmapped would turn these into immediate, precisely-located faults and would likely have caught this in one run instead of five.

message: FIXED the container: our own manual guard was range-checking a VTABLE pointer against the HEAP range, so the allocator-owner lookup rejected its only registered entry and returned NULL every time. Widening the range populates the container (slots all-NULL to real objects) and heap_allocs jumps 23 -> 49. Coverage is mixed (reached 101 -> 86, 22 gained / 37 lost) so this is kept on the #72 precedent, not as a clean win.
note: 2026-08-08, ledger #89, completing #86-#88. THE BUG WAS OURS, NOT THE GAME'S. sub_001E8E20 ("which allocator owns this pointer?") walks two registries; registry A at 0x5BC53C is EMPTY (its loop probe never fired) and registry B at 0x5BC538 holds exactly ONE entry, 0x01088A90. A manual guard we had added did `eax = MEM32(esi); if (!(eax >= 0x00880000u && eax < 0x04000000u)) goto skip;` - that is the HEAP range, but eax is the entry's VTABLE pointer and vtables live in the image (.rdata), far BELOW the heap. Proven rather than inferred: "[G] entry=0x01088A90 vtable=0x003F4770 passes_heap_guard=0" on all eight calls. So the walk skipped its only entry, returned NULL, and #88's chain followed - sub_00202B87 dereferenced that NULL, guest VA 0 being mapped meant nothing faulted, the block-size query answered 0, capacity read 0, and every array grow zeroed from slot 0 and wiped the whole array. FIX: widen to 0x00010000u..0x04000000u (image base to end of guest RAM) at both sites, loc_001E8E41 and loc_001E8E7F. ALSO CLEANED UP: the loc_001E8E41 guard had EIGHT accumulated copies from repeated tool runs, four of them jumping to loc_001E8E99 - the SECOND walk's label, wrong for that walk. Collapsed to one. message: Probed the sub_00205170 wall: root cause is a NULL container walked out of mapped guest page 0
note: Ledger #114. No behaviour change - this is a diagnosis, so the zero delta is expected; tree stripped of probes, rebuilt and re-verified deterministic 2 of 2 at reached 157 / callsites 437 / 274 kernel calls / 91 heap allocs / 8 safe stubs, same crash. CHAIN, every link probed: sub_001F7930 runs on 0x01098400 and 0x01098870 whose container MEM32(this+0x28) is NULL (measured BEFORE the icall - the first probe sat after it and could have been reading a clobbered edi). Guest VA 0 is mapped, so the count comes from MEM32(0xC) non-zero and the element array from MEM32(0x8), and the loop dispatches virtual +0x64 on junk page-0 words: 0, 1, 0x44, 0x003DA978 (that last one appears verbatim in triage's failed-icall list). Index 6 holds 0x0120E000, a REAL object with the real vtable 0x003F4770, so that dispatch succeeds and reaches sub_0020A8B0 - which the XBE scan proves is the correct virtual for that class, appearing at exactly one VA in .rdata, 0x003F47D4 = 0x003F4770+0x64. sub_00205170 then hits a SECOND null: MEM32(this+0x70) is 0, MEM32(0) reads mapped page 0 non-zero so the early-out never fires, count>>3 = 0 puts the cursor at guest 0x4 with end bound 0xFFFFFFFC, and it picks 0x44 out of page 0 as a heap block - matching esi=0x44 in the crash dump exactly. Twelve base-class allocator objects (0x0120D000..0x01218000, one page apart, heap allocs #76-#87) are built by sub_00234E18 and never get a pool: their init is vtable+0x24 = sub_002036E0, while the only writer of +0x70 is sub_00211280, which fires exactly ONCE all boot, on 0x01088A90. Those twelve are a SECONDARY hazard - 0x0120E000 was scavenged from page 0, not legitimately in the container. NEXT: find who should set MEM32(this+0x28) = this+0x68 (five of the six healthy outers have exactly that relationship) on 0x01098400 and 0x01098870. TOOLING LIMIT, and it nearly caused a false finding: a trace-mode watch on 0x0120E070 reported nothing at all for the whole boot, not even the guaranteed heap zero-fill of that page, while watching offset 0 of the same page caught all three writes and a control at 0x01088B00 (+0xB00) worked fine.
