That also withdraws the claim in (6) that wall 42 shares wall 41's unpopulated-metaobject root cause: the structural resemblance of the metafield walk is real, but nothing places it on this path, so 42 must not be counted in that family until a probe puts it there. WHAT SURVIVES: points (1) through (4), which rest on their own probe evidence - FUN_0020AA90 is dlmalloc free, FUN_0020EEE0 frees its param_1, FUN_0020EF90 passes its own this, and the software poll named the writer. The honest statement of wall 42 is now narrower and true: a CONFIRMED use-after-free of 01092B58 with an UNIDENTIFIED caller. NEXT: identify the real callers of the three FUN_0020EF90 calls, and write no mechanism down again before a probe names them. This is the second time on this wall that a tidy mechanism outran the evidence; the first was reading the page watchpoint's 33 zeros as 'the object is not here'.

message: PC modernisation, no boot change: Xbox RAM is now a 64/128 MB setting, payloads moved to a dedicated arena below the 256 MB hardware ceiling, and high-resolution texture replacement landed with generated mip chains, verified 512/1K/2K/4K with 8192 rejected
note: COUNTERS UNCHANGED AND NOT RE-RUN - none of this touches the boot path, and all of it is off by default. The figures carried here are the previous entry's; this entry records infrastructure, not progress into the boot, and must not be read as either. Verified through tools/gfx_harness (all 5 stages PASS), which is the only way any of it could be exercised, since the game does not reach rendering. (1) THE RULE THAT DROVE IT: a console limit may become a PC setting only when HOST code we write enforces it; when the translated GUEST binary performs arithmetic that assumes it, it cannot move. (2) RAM: XBOX_TOTAL_RAM was a compile-time 64 MB, now g_xbox_total_ram set by xbox_ConfigureRam() from XBOX_RAM_MB; kernel_memory.c derives TotalPhysicalPages from it. Accepts 64 or 128 ONLY, deliberately: the guest assumes a 26-bit bus where RAM wraps modulo 64 MB, which the port reproduces with mirrored views, so an arbitrary size would put the mirror where the guest's arithmetic does not expect it. 128 MB is the one larger layout the hardware itself defined. (3) PAYLOADS: moved to XBOX_PAYLOAD_BASE 0x0C000000 - XBOX_PAYLOAD_LIMIT 0x10000000, sized by XBOX_PAYLOAD_MB; d3d8_PayloadAlloc() takes the arena first and falls back to the guest heap. The 256 MB ceiling above it is HARDWARE and stays documented rather than exposed: the binary masks resource pointers with & 0x0FFFFFFF, 28 bits, in thousands of places. (4) TEXTURE REPLACEMENT (src/d3d/d3d8_texrepl.c): replacements are HOST memory and never enter the guest address space, so no Xbox limit applies to them at all. Identity is an FNV-1a hash of the game's own level-0 pixels at upload rather than a filename, so replacement is independent of the .igb asset pipeline; the miss log line names the file to supply and is the whole authoring interface. 32-bit uncompressed BMP, chosen over DDS because DDS needs a parser for a large format or an external library. Negative lookups are cached so a texture re-uploaded every frame does not stat a missing file every frame. (5) SIZES, each verified by a real run from a 64x64 original: 512x512 = 1.3 MB, 1024x1024 = 5.3 MB, 2048x2048 = 21.3 MB, 4096x4096 = 85.3 MB of VRAM with mips; 8192x1024 rejected by the guard. Only an UPPER bound is enforced, TEXREPL_MAX_DIM 4096 - there is no lower bound, so art can arrive one resolution at a time. The ceiling is POLICY, not hardware: D3D11 feature level 11 permits 16384, but each step up is 4x the memory of the one below, so a few dozen 4K replacements would exhaust a mid-range card for detail nobody can resolve. One edit to change, and the reasoning is in the header so the next reader can weigh it. (6) MIPS ARE MANDATORY at these magnifications, not a nicety: a 4K texture standing in for a 64x64 original is minified enormously and unmipped would alias and crawl in motion, i.e. look WORSE than the texture it replaced. That forces the creation path, because a mip chain cannot be generated on an IMMUTABLE texture created with initial data: MipLevels=0, USAGE_DEFAULT, BIND_RENDER_TARGET, MISC_GENERATE_MIPS, upload level 0, then GenerateMips. g_texrepl_vram_bytes tracks the cost because silent VRAM exhaustion is hard to diagnose. (7) TOOLING: COBJMACROS must be defined before d3d11.h or the ID3D11Device_* names compile as implicit calls and fail at link with unresolved externals. Two python heredoc edits corrupted backslash escapes in C string literals - the documented trap - and were redone with line-indexed edits and fputc(10, stderr) instead of an embedded newline escape. NEXT: unchanged and unaffected - identify the real callers of the three FUN_0020EF90 calls at wall 42.

message: Wall 42 callers identified, and my own retraction was WRONG: the recursion is real. Three DIFFERENT objects sharing one holder each reach refcount zero and each free it, so the holder at 01092B58 is freed on the first release and used twice more
note: DIAGNOSIS ONLY - no guard, probes stripped after the run. Counters carried from the wall-42 entry; this run was probe-instrumented and not a clean measurement. (1) THE RETRACTION IN ENTRY 166 IS ITSELF WITHDRAWN. It argued that FUN_001EA640 is entered only 4 times on 4 objects, none of them the holder, therefore it cannot be the recursive walk releasing the holder. That is a NON-SEQUITUR: a teardown walking object A releases A's FIELDS, which are necessarily different objects from A. Different `this` was never evidence against the recursion. Both facts are true at once and were reproduced in ONE build: [EA640] enter this=01097858 / 010978C0 / 01097F28 / 01096BB8 (4 entries, other objects) while [EF90] enter this=01092B58 three times. (2) THE REAL CALLERS, from CaptureStackBackTrace at sub_0020EF90 entry, symbolised against the linker map. All three calls: sub_0020EF90 <- sub_00123600+0xC9 <- sub_00217FF0+0xD6. Call #1 then <- sub_001EA6B0+0x620. Call #2 <- sub_001EA640+0x48E <- sub_001F8180+0x9F <- sub_001EA6B0+0x620. Call #3 <- that pair TWICE <- sub_001EA6B0+0x620. So the repetition is a recursive descent rooted at sub_001EA6B0 recursing through sub_001F8180/sub_001EA640 at depths 0, 1, 2. sub_001EA6B0 is NEW - it was never in the record. (3) THE BACKTRACE WAS VALIDATED BEFORE BEING BELIEVED, because it had been doubted twice: (a) ICF folding does occur in this build - 255 addresses carry more than one sub_ name, one of them 224 names - but NONE of the eight functions on this path is folded, each has a unique address; (b) every frame offset lies inside its function's host extent, and there is no unlisted symbol between sub_001EA640 (0x140DE17F0) and sub_001EA6B0 (0x140DE2140), so +0x48E is genuinely inside sub_001EA640. (4) THE HOLDER IS NOT RELEASED THREE TIMES - THREE DIFFERENT OBJECTS ARE. sub_00123600 reads `MEM32(ecx+4) -= 1; if (refs == 0) { ecx = MEM32(ecx); sub_0020EF90(); }` - it decrements the OBJECT's refcount and passes the object's field0 as `this`. Three distinct objects each hit zero and each name 01092B58 in field0. The holder is their common owner. (5) sub_0020EEE0 DOES FREE THE HOLDER, confirmed by reading rather than inference. sub_0020EF90 calls it with this = MEM32(holder) (the table) and param_1 = holder, guarded by `if (MEM8(holder+0x20) != 0)` - and that flag read 01 on all three calls. Inside sub_0020EEE0 the stack is [esp+0]=saved esi, [esp+4]=saved ecx, [esp+8]=return address, [esp+0xC]=param_1, so the `esi = MEM32(esp + 0xC)` at loc_0020EF01 reloads THE HOLDER, and loc_0020EF4A then calls sub_001E8E20(esi) to find its pool and frees it through pool vtbl+0xFC. It also frees MEM32(holder+0x10) first. (6) SO THE MECHANISM IS COMPLETE: call #1 frees the holder; calls #2 and #3 operate on freed memory; by #3 the allocator's free-list link has overwritten field0, which is exactly the observed 01091B30 -> 01091B30 -> 0109863C, and matches the earlier finding that the writer is the dlmalloc free path sub_0020AA90. sub_001EB890 then binary- searches a table read out of a freed block and faults. (7) THE DEFECT IS THAT THE HOLDER IS FREED ON THE FIRST RELEASE WHILE TWO OBJECTS STILL REFERENCE IT. The holder is not refcounted at all here; the free is gated only by MEM8(holder+0x20), and by `MEM32(table+0x14) > 0` at loc_0020EEFA. NEXT AND UNPROVEN: +0x14 looks like an entry count, and sub_001EBA30 removes the entry immediately before. If that count is one of the containers that is sized but never populated - the wall 40/41 defect - the guard would pass when it should not. PROBE IT: print MEM32(table+0x14) and MEM8(holder+0x20) on each of the three calls before concluding anything. Do NOT guard sub_001EB890; that would hide the free. (8) METHOD NOTE: this is the third position taken on wall 42. The first two each rested on a single instrument. This one rests on two independent probes in the same build plus two structural checks on the symbolisation, and it explains every number previously observed instead of discarding some of them.

message: Wall 42's link to the walls 40/41 family is REFUTED by probe: table+0x14 is populated (0 then 1), not sized-but-empty. The free fires on call #2, not #1 - count=0 skips it, count=1 executes it - so the holder is freed with a third object still referencing it
note: DIAGNOSIS ONLY - probes stripped after the run, no guard applied. Crash unchanged at sub_001EB890+0x1D5 (RVA 0xDEE205), fault 0x8B0146F4. This entry REFUTES the hypothesis recorded in the previous one, which is the outcome it was designed to be able to produce. (1) THE PROBE. Two probes in one build: at sub_0020EF90 entry printing this/obj/table/table+0x14/holder+0x20, and at loc_0020EEFA in sub_0020EEE0 printing the guard it actually tests. Result, verbatim: [EF90] this=01092B58 obj=0121F000 table=01091B30 count=0 flag=01 / this=01092B58 obj=011F0000 table=01091B30 count=1 flag=01 / this=01092B58 obj=011D2000 table=0109863C count=4160656 flag=01. [EEE0] guard table=01091B30 count=0 / guard table=01091B30 count=1. (2) THE HYPOTHESIS IS DEAD. table+0x14 reads 0 on the first call and 1 on the second - it is being POPULATED, not left empty. The walls 40/41 defect is a container that is sized and never filled; this is not that. Wall 42 must NOT be counted in that family, and the root-defect record has been corrected to say so. Fixing the metaobject setup will not retire this wall. (3) WHAT THE GUARD ACTUALLY DOES, which is the opposite of what was assumed. sub_0020EEE0 opens with `eax = MEM32(esi+0x14); if (eax <= 0) goto loc_0020EF65`, so count=0 SKIPS the whole body. On call #1 the free is therefore NOT taken. On call #2 count=1 and the free IS taken. The previous entry said call #1 frees the holder; that was wrong by one call, and only the probe could have caught it. (4) CORRECTED SEQUENCE. Call #1: count=0, free skipped, holder intact. Call #2: count=1, free executed, holder 01092B58 released through its pool's vtbl+0xFC while a THIRD object still holds it in field0. Call #3: the holder is freed memory - field0 now reads 0109863C, the allocator's free-list link, and table+0x14 reads garbage 4160656 - and sub_001EBA30 walks that table into sub_001EB890, which faults. Note call #3 never reaches sub_0020EEE0 at all (only two [EEE0] lines), because it dies earlier in sub_001EBA30; that is consistent with the crash site and is why the flag=01 on call #3 leads nowhere. (5) THE DEFECT, STATED NARROWLY: three distinct objects (0121F000, 011F0000, 011D2000 - all page-aligned, worth noting) each reach refcount zero and each name 01092B58 in field0. Removing the second one frees that shared object. Nothing refcounts the holder itself; its destruction is gated only by another object's count field and by MEM8(holder+0x20), which is 01 throughout. (6) NEXT. Two questions, in order. Why do three objects share one holder - is field0 an owner pointer that should be refcounted, or should these be three separate holders? And is MEM8(holder+0x20) - the auto-release flag, set legitimately by sub_001F8830 under the descriptor constructor sub_00216EE0 - correct for an object with multiple referents? Do NOT guard sub_001EB890; that hides the free. (7) METHOD: the previous entry named this probe as the thing that would decide the family question and said explicitly that it was a probe and not a finding. It came back negative. Recording the refutation as prominently as a confirmation is the point.

message: Wall 42's shared holder identified: it is a 16 KB memory POOL, and the three objects are the class metaobjects igObject / igMetaField / igBoolMetaField allocated through it. The sharing is correct by design - the defect is that destroying one pooled object frees the pool
note: DIAGNOSIS ONLY - probes stripped, no guard, crash unchanged at sub_001EB890+0x1D5. (1) THE THREE OBJECTS ARE CLASSES. sub_0020EF90 does strlen(obj+8), so these objects carry a name there. Printed: obj=0121F000 'igBoolMetaField', obj=011F0000 'igMetaField', obj=011D2000 'igObject'. They are Alchemy class metaobjects, and page-aligned because they are page allocations. (2) THE HOLDER IS AN ALLOCATOR, established by dumping it. holder=01092B58: [0C]=00004000 capacity, [10]=01092B80 base, [14]=01096B80 current, [18]=01096B80 end, [1C]=FFFFFFFF, [20]=00000001 flag. The arithmetic is exact and self-consistent: holder+0x28 == 01092B80 == base, and base + 0x4000 == 01096B80 == current == end. So it is a 0x28-byte header followed by a 16 KB inline arena, and current == end means THE POOL IS EXHAUSTED. (3) SO THE SHARING IS CORRECT AND IS NOT THE BUG. field0 is the back-pointer to the allocator that owns the object - the same relationship sub_001E8E20 (get-containing-pool) exists to answer. Three objects share it because all three were allocated through it. A correction to my own guess: the objects are NOT inside [01092B80, 01096B80); that 16 KB is the pool's own bookkeeping arena, and the page-aligned objects live elsewhere, which fits a pool that hands out pages and maintains a pointer->pool map. (4) THE DEFECT RESTATED: destroying ONE pooled object destroys the POOL. sub_0020EF90 ends with `if (MEM8(pool+0x20)) sub_0020EEE0(this = pool->table, param_1 = pool)` and that flag reads 1, so unregistering the second class frees the pool while two other classes still name it in field0. Calls #2 and #3 then run on freed memory. (5) THE TABLE'S COUNTERS CORROBORATE THE SEQUENCE: tbl=01091B30 with t[04] decrementing 0x42 -> 0x41 per unregistration and t[14] - the guard sub_0020EEE0 tests - going 0 -> 1. After the free the same read yields tbl=0109863C, t[00]=0C000181, t[10]=0x680, which is the allocator free-list residue the earlier record described as 'a count field holding a pointer and an array field holding 0x680'. (6) A REAL LINK TO THE ROOT DEFECT, and a different one from the theory refuted in the previous entry: pool[0x1C] reads FFFFFFFF - the same -1 'size unknown' marker that runs through the walls 40-42 chain, where sub_00216FD0 is recorded as the function that fills in the real size. An allocator carrying -1 where a size belongs, which has also run itself to exhaustion, is worth chasing on its own. (7) NEXT: find who writes pool+0x1C (guest 0x01092B74) and whether it is ever written at all, since an uninitialised -1 and a deliberately-marked -1 have different fixes. Then ask why MEM8(pool+0x20) is set on a pool with multiple live objects. Do NOT guard sub_001EB890.

message: The -1 is plain constructor initialisation, written once by sub_001F8830 and never filled in. Reading that constructor CORRECTS the previous entry twice: the pool is NOT exhausted (current==end is its initial state) and field0 is the PARENT ALLOCATOR, not a table
note: DIAGNOSTIC WATCH BUILD - do not measure progress on it. Software poll on guest 0x01092B74 (pool+0x1C). (1) THE WRITE, ONCE ONLY: 00000000 -> FFFFFFFF, and no second write for the object's whole life. The page watchpoint again reported MISSED WRITES and is again untrustworthy; the poll is what caught it. (2) THE WRITER, from the poll's backtrace symbolised against build_watch's OWN map (a different build means a different map - using build/'s map here would misname every frame): sub_001F8830+0x31C <- sub_00202D89 <- sub_00202D14 <- sub_00123590 <- sub_00216EE0+0x2E8 <- sub_00222708+0x20A <- sub_002235D0+0x541 <- sub_002221E0+0x13A <- sub_00209650 <- sub_002366BC <- sub_0023666F <- sub_00239E50. That is the descriptor constructor sub_00216EE0 at essentially the documented +0x2e3 offset, under sub_00222708, on the CREATE path of the first type module - exactly the path TYPE_DESCRIPTOR.md describes. (3) IT IS INITIALISATION, NOT A DEFECT SIGNAL. sub_001F8830 is a constructor and writes the field unconditionally: this[0]=arg2, [4]=0, [8]=arg1, [0C]=arg3, [10]=[14]=[18]=0, [1C]=-1, [20]=1. The -1 and the auto-release flag are set side by side, three instructions apart, with no condition. This corroborates the earlier finding that the +0x20 flag is legitimate initialisation. (4) CORRECTION 1 - THE POOL IS NOT EXHAUSTED. The previous entry read current==end==base+0x4000 as exhaustion. The constructor's tail sets exactly that as the INITIAL state: it calls the parent's allocate through vtbl+0xCC, then `this[0x10]=base; eax=base+capacity; this[0x18]=eax; this[0x14]=eax`. So current==end is how the allocator STARTS - it fills downward. It then writes a trailer at the top, MEM16(end-4)=0 and MEM16(end-2)=capacity>>2, a free-block descriptor in dword units. Nothing about the pool being full is supported. (5) CORRECTION 2 - FIELD0 IS THE PARENT ALLOCATOR, NOT A TABLE. this[0]=arg2, and the constructor immediately does `eax=MEM32(arg2); ecx=MEM32(eax+0xC); eax=MEM32(ecx);` then icalls [eax+0xCC] to obtain the 0x4000 block. arg2 is therefore an object with a vtable that allocates - the parent. Everything previously called 'the table' (01091B30) is that parent allocator, which also means the guard in sub_0020EEE0, MEM32(this+0x14), is the PARENT'S field, not a table's entry count. The 0x42->0x41 and 0->1 readings need re-reading in that light. (6) A DEAD END WORTH RECORDING: grepping the lifted code for readers of '+0x1C' returns 4333 hits binary-wide, including sub_001EB890 itself, which looked like a direct link from the -1 to the crash. It is not: those matches are MEM32(esp + 0x1C), a STACK SLOT, not an object field. Offset-only greps do not discriminate here and must be filtered for the base register before they mean anything. (7) NEXT: the -1 is only interesting if something reads it. Find the pool class's own methods via its vtable rather than by offset grep, and identify what field +0x1C is. Also re-derive sub_0020EEE0's guard now that its `this` is known to be the parent allocator.

message: The destroy decision is a counter NOTHING EVER INITIALISES: parent+0x14 is 0, and the only write to it in the whole run is sub_0020EEE0's own skip path incrementing it 0->1. So the first removal is skipped and every removal after it destroys the pool. My earlier refutation of the walls 40/41 link is VOID
note: DIAGNOSTIC WATCH BUILD. Software poll armed on guest 0x01091B44 (parent+0x14) for the whole run: exactly ONE change reported. (1) THE DECISION SITE, read in full. sub_0020EEE0 opens `eax = MEM32(esi+0x14); if (eax <= 0) goto loc_0020EF65`, and loc_0020EF65 is `eax++; MEM32(esi+0x14) = eax;`. So the branch that SKIPS the destroy is the branch that increments the counter gating it. Read as a state machine: count 0 -> skip and set 1; count 1 -> unlink and free. The first removal is spared and EVERY REMOVAL AFTER IT DESTROYS THE POOL. (2) NOTHING ELSE EVER WRITES IT. The poll was armed for the entire run and reported one change, '00000000 -> 00000001 across sub_0020EEE0', with the backtrace on call #1's own stack (sub_0020EF90+0x238 <- sub_00123600+0xD5 <- sub_00217FF0+0xE2 <- sub_001EA6B0+0x64F). No owner, no registration, no constructor ever sets this field. It is 0 because nothing initialised it. (3) SO MY REFUTATION IN THE EARLIER ENTRY IS VOID. That entry argued wall 42 is NOT in the walls 40/41 family because +0x14 'reads 0 then 1, it is being POPULATED, not left empty'. The 0->1 is this function incrementing its own guard. The premise was wrong, so the refutation carries no weight and is withdrawn. What is NOT thereby proven is the positive claim - that something SHOULD write parent+0x14 - so wall 42 still must not be recorded as a member of that family. The door is reopened, not walked through. (4) THE CRASH IS NOW EXPLAINED END TO END. sub_0020EF90(pool, obj) does three things: sub_001F87A0(this = pool->field0, obj) which calls sub_001EB890 with obj+8 - the NAME string - i.e. a name lookup in the parent allocator's index; then sub_001EBA30(this = pool, obj, strlen+9) which returns the block to the pool, walking the 16-bit trailer descriptors the constructor laid down; then the conditional destroy. On call #3 the pool has already been freed, so pool->field0 reads 0109863C - free-list residue - and the name lookup runs against a garbage allocator. THAT is the fault at sub_001EB890+0x1D5. (5) THE THREE OBJECTS ARE POOL BLOCKS, not polymorphic objects. block[0] = owning pool, block[4] = refcount (sub_00123600 decrements exactly that), block[8] = NUL-terminated name. The pool likewise has no vtable - its field0 is the parent allocator - so the plan to enumerate the pool class's methods through a vtable is dead: there is no vtable to walk. (6) NEXT: find whether anything in the binary writes parent+0x14 at all - a static search for stores to +0x14 with the parent's base register, not an offset grep, since offset-only greps match MEM32(esp + 0x14) stack slots and already produced one false lead. If nothing writes it, the field is uninitialised by construction and that is the defect; if something does and never ran, that is the walls 40/41 pattern and the family link is real.

message: Nothing initialises parent+0x14: dynamically the only write all run is sub_0020EEE0's own increment, and statically the two functions that DO initialise this field write it as part of a (capacity, base, current) triple - the parent has the first two set and the third zero
note: Static search plus the earlier watch run. Answers the question 'does anything write parent+0x14 at all'. (1) DYNAMICALLY, NO. The software poll was armed on guest 0x01091B44 for the whole boot and reported exactly one change: 0 -> 1 from sub_0020EEE0's own skip path. No constructor, owner or registration touches it. (2) STATICALLY, THREE FUNCTIONS in the allocator cluster write +0x14 through an object register: sub_001F8830 (the pool constructor: this[0x14]=0, then this[0x14]=base+capacity), sub_0020AE10 (writes [0xC], [0x10] and [0x14]=base+0x400 as a group), and sub_0020EEE0 (the self-increment). Binary-wide the same filtered search gives 1148 sites in 763 functions, but +0x14 is a generic offset shared by hundreds of unrelated classes, so that number means nothing on its own - it is reported only so the next reader does not repeat the search expecting it to. (3) THE SUGGESTIVE PART. Both real initialisers write +0x14 as the third member of a (capacity at +0x0C, base at +0x10, current at +0x14) triple. The parent 01091B30 has [0x0C]=0x400 and [0x10]=01091B50 SET and [0x14]=0. Note 01091B30 + 0x20 == 01091B50, so its base is its own header+0x20, exactly the pattern the pool follows with a 0x28 header - and by that pattern [0x14] should read base+capacity = 01091F50, not 0. (4) NOT PROVEN, AND THIS IS THE GAP: nothing yet establishes that 01091B30 is of the same class as the objects those two functions construct. Same shape is not same class. Until that is shown, 'the third field was never written' is a strong lead and not a finding. (5) A METHOD CORRECTION WORTH KEEPING. The write of 01091B50 into parent+0x10 was attributed by the poll to frame sub_00202D89+0x1E9, but reading sub_00202D89 shows it contains NO store to +0x10 - only esi[0] and esi[4]. The poll fires after a call returns, so the real write happened inside the icall [edx+0xCC] that frame makes, i.e. inside the allocator's own allocate routine. A poll frame bounds a subtree; it does not name a writer. The same caveat is already recorded for this instrument and was nearly forgotten again. (6) ALSO: an earlier regex here used e[abcds][ixp] to mean 'object register', which matches ESP. That polluted the first pass with stack-slot stores. Filter base registers by explicit alternation - eax|ebx|ecx|edx|esi|edi. (7) NEXT: identify 01091B30's class. sub_00202D89 allocates a 0x24-byte block via the parent's vtbl+0xCC and hands it to sub_001F8830, so the parent is the ALLOCATOR being called, not the object constructed. Watch the parent's own construction, or find what vtable sits above it, before assuming its layout.

message: The wall-42 objects are Alchemy's memory-pool family: the SDK's igMemoryPool carries _rawMemory/_lowMemory/_highMemory followed by bool _isOwnedMemory, matching the measured [0x10]/[0x14]/[0x18] plus the byte flag at [0x20] that gates the free. Also corrects the pool's shape - a 0x24-byte object, not a header over an inline arena
note: (1) STRUCTURE, from the game rather than the SDK. par=01091B30, par[0]=01091B18 (call it B18), and B18 is a small record: B18[0]=par, B18[4]=01092B58 (THE POOL), B18[8]=0x4000 (the pool's capacity), B18[0xC]=01088A90 (an object with a real vtable at guest 0x003F4770), B18[0x10]=0. So B18 is a list header and the pool is the entry in it. That also settles sub_0020EEE0's unlink: `eax=MEM32(par); ecx=MEM32(eax+4)` gives ecx=THE POOL, which equals param_1, so it takes the head-removal branch loc_0020EF0E, not the middle-unlink branch. An earlier reading that the middle branch would write through a NULL prev - a page-zero write - is therefore NOT reached, and was never recorded as fact. (2) NO RTTI FOR THIS CLASS. The runtime vtable 0x003F4770 has no complete-object-locator (vt-4 reads 0) and does not appear in the 743-vtable RTTI export, which covers 0x003E173C then jumps to 0x0042A7DC. So the class cannot be named from RTTI. (3) WHAT THE SDK GIVES SAFELY. Alchemy 5.0's igCore has igMemoryPool, igArenaMemoryPool, igAliasMemoryPool, igInternalMemoryPoolList and igMemoryPoolInfo - the family these objects belong to. 5.0's igMemoryPool is far larger than a 0x24-byte object and the game shipped on 3.0, so offsets MUST NOT be mapped across; that is exactly the misattribution trap already recorded for SDK-derived names. What is legitimate is the SHAPE: igMemoryPool declares _rawMemory, _lowMemory, _highMemory consecutively and follows them with the bools _isAlchemyMemory and _isOwnedMemory. The measured object has three pointers at [0x10]/[0x14]/[0x18] followed by a BYTE flag at [0x20] written with MEM8. (4) THAT MAKES SENSE OF THE FREE. sub_0020EEE0 frees MEM32(pool+0x10) first and then the pool itself - i.e. it frees the raw memory and then the object, which is what a pool destructor does, and it is gated by the byte at +0x20. A flag meaning 'I own this memory' gating a free of exactly that memory is a coherent reading, and the constructor sets it to 1 unconditionally. Stated as a strong structural correspondence, NOT as a named-field identification. (5) CORRECTION: THE POOL IS NOT A HEADER OVER AN INLINE ARENA. An earlier entry described a 0x28-byte header followed by 16 KB of inline storage, because base == pool+0x28. sub_00202D89 allocates exactly 0x24 bytes for the object, and sub_001F8830 obtains the 0x4000 block by calling the allocator's vtbl+0xCC and storing the result in [0x10]. The block is a SEPARATE allocation that merely landed adjacent. By the same token the earlier dump's pool[0x24] and pool[0x28] are the next heap chunk's header, not pool fields, and should be ignored. (6) NEXT: par is a different class from the pool - its [0x14] is incremented as an integer, so it cannot be a _lowMemory pointer. Find what allocates par and what else reads par+0x04 (0x42, decrementing per removal) and par+0x08 (0x40), since those two look like a count against a capacity and 0x42 > 0x40 already.

message: par is a sorted array with binary search, and the 66-vs-64 reading was NOT an overflow: +0x08 is the binary-search seed (largest power of two <= count), +0x0C is the real capacity at 1024. Reading sub_00204800 killed the overflow hypothesis before it was recorded as a finding
note: (1) MEASURED FIRST. Watch on par+0x04 for a whole run: 66 increments, all 'across sub_00204800', then two decrements 0x42 -> 0x41 -> 0x40 at the wall-42 removals. Watch on par+0x08: seven changes, 1 2 4 8 10 20 40 - doubling - also all from sub_00204800. Watch on par+0x10 (base): exactly ONE change, 0 -> 01091B50, so the storage never moved. The array holds 4-byte page pointers (011EF000, 0120C000, 011EA000, ... at 4-byte stride). (2) THE TEMPTING WRONG READING. count 66 against a doubling 'capacity' of 64, with storage that never reallocated, looks exactly like a container overrun by two entries - the walls 40/41 signature. It is not, and reading the function is what settled it. (3) sub_00204800 IS AN ORDERED INSERT. It grows only when count == this[0x0C]: `edi = cap+cap; sub_00203450(base, edi*4)` then `this[0x10] = newbase; this[0x0C] = edi`. It then memmoves the tail right by one entry via sub_00342AA0 and stores the new value at the insertion index. So THIS[0x0C] IS THE CAPACITY, in entries, and it reads 0x400 = 1024. Count 66 is nowhere near it, which is exactly why the base never moved: no growth was ever needed. par[0x0C]=0x400 is 1024 ENTRIES, not 1024 bytes as an earlier note assumed. (4) WHAT +0x08 REALLY IS. The function's tail: `count++; eax = this[8]; if (2*eax > count) return; if (eax == 0) this[8] = 1 else this[8] = 2*eax`. That keeps this[8] at the largest power of two <= count - the seed a binary search starts from. With count 66 it is 64, which is correct, not two short of anything. It also corroborates that sub_001EB890 is a binary search over this array, which is what it is called to do. (5) NO DEFECT HERE. The 66/64 relationship is by design. The overflow hypothesis is refuted and no guard or fix is warranted at this site. Recording the negative because the reasoning that produced it - three watch runs and a read - is the same reasoning that would have justified a wrong fix if the read had been skipped. (6) par's LAYOUT, as far as it is now established: [0x04] count, [0x08] binary-search seed, [0x0C] capacity in entries, [0x10] base pointer. Unaccounted: [0x14] (the destroy gate, 0, nothing initialises it), [0x18] (0), [0x1C] (00020003, looks like a packed pair). (7) NEXT, UNCHANGED AND SHARPER: par+0x14 is not part of the array bookkeeping at all, so its zero is not explained by anything found here. It remains the field that decides whether the pool is destroyed, and nothing writes it but sub_0020EEE0 itself.

message: par+0x1C is not a field at all - it is the allocator's chunk header for the array block, written twice by sub_0020F860. That closes par's layout: a 7-dword object whose only unexplained fields are +0x14, the destroy gate, and +0x18, both zero
note: (1) THE ARITHMETIC CAME FIRST AND WAS SUSPICIOUS ON ITS OWN. par+0x1C == 01091B4C == the array base 01091B50 minus 4, and pool+0x24 == 01092B7C == the pool's block base 01092B80 minus 4. Two 'fields' each sitting exactly one dword below a block base, both with values ending in 3, is the shape of an allocator header rather than object state. (2) CONFIRMED BY WATCH, not by the resemblance. Poll on guest 0x01091B4C for a whole run: exactly two changes, both 'across sub_0020F860', an allocator routine - 00000000 -> 007C9601 -> 00020003. No object method ever writes it. The low bits are flags (1 then 3) and the remainder is a size: 0x007C9600 = ~7.8 MB, then 0x00020000 = 128 KB, which is a large free region being carved down. Classic dlmalloc size|flags. (3) SO PAR'S OBJECT ENDS AT 0x1C AND ITS LAYOUT IS NOW CLOSED - seven dwords: [0x00] pointer to the B18 list header, [0x04] count, [0x08] binary-search seed, [0x0C] capacity in entries, [0x10] base pointer, [0x14] the gate sub_0020EEE0 tests to decide whether to destroy the pool, [0x18] unexplained. Both of the last two read zero. (4) THIRD INSTANCE OF THE SAME MISTAKE THIS SESSION, so it is worth stating as a rule: when dumping an object, everything at or past the allocation's end is the NEXT block's allocator metadata, not object state. It already produced 'pool+0x24 = 00080003' and 'the pool is a 0x28-byte header over an inline arena', both wrong. Establish the object's SIZE - from its allocation call, or from where a following block's base sits - before reading any offset near the end. (5) WHERE THIS LEAVES WALL 42. Every field of par is now accounted for except +0x14 and +0x18. +0x14 is the destroy gate; nothing in the binary initialises it, and the only write all run is sub_0020EEE0 incrementing it on the branch that skips the destroy. That remains the whole question, and it is now isolated: it cannot be array bookkeeping, it cannot be allocator metadata, and it is not written by any constructor. (6) NEXT: +0x18 is the only remaining unknown and sits adjacent to the gate. Watch guest 0x01091B48 for the run. If it is also never written, the two form an uninitialised pair at the end of the object, which points at the constructor rather than at any caller.

message: par+0x18 is never written by guest code at all, and chasing it exposed a NEW failure mode in the page watchpoint: it MISATTRIBUTES a write's rip, not just misses writes. It named a constructor that a direct probe proves runs once, on a different object, on a different page
note: (1) THE ANSWER. Poll on guest 0x01091B48 (par+0x18) for a whole run: ZERO changes. The only accesses at all are four byte-wide 0 -> 0 writes from a rip outside the module (rva 0x3D2A4E579), i.e. a host-side zeroing of the freshly committed memory. No guest code ever writes it. Unlike every other watch this session the summary line agreed with the poll - last seen 0, actually 0, no MISSED WRITES - so for once both instruments concur. (2) THE TRAP. The earlier par+0x14 run had also logged two module-level writes of 0 -> 0, at rva 0x102D13A and 0xF6E636. Symbolised they are sub_00211530+0x3A9A (the allocator) and sub_001F8830+0x166 - THE POOL CONSTRUCTOR. That reads as 'the constructor explicitly initialises the gate to zero', which would have made the gate's zero intentional and sent the investigation somewhere else entirely. (3) BOTH STRUCTURAL CHECKS PASSED, so the symbolisation was not the problem: neither function is ICF-folded (one name each at its address) and both offsets fall inside their host extents (0x166 of 0x420, 0x3A9A of 0x5FC0). (4) A DIRECT PROBE REFUTES IT ANYWAY. Probing sub_001F8830's entry for the whole boot: it is entered EXACTLY ONCE, with this=01092B58 (the pool), arg1=0, arg2=01091B30 (par), arg3=0x4000. It is never called on par. (5) AND IT IS PHYSICALLY IMPOSSIBLE. sub_001F8830 writes only this+0x00..0x20 with this=01092B58, so every store it makes lands on page 0x01092000. The watched address is on page 0x01091000. A page-protection watchpoint faults on the watched page; that function cannot fault on it at all. (6) SO THE PAGE WATCHPOINT MISATTRIBUTES RIPS. The instrument was already recorded as unreliable for MISSING writes (its own MISSED WRITES banner). This is a second, worse failure: a write it does report can carry a rip that belongs to neither the writing instruction nor the watched page. Do not symbolise its rips at all. The software poll remains the trustworthy instrument, and it is the one that gave both real answers here - one change on +0x14, none on +0x18. (7) WHAT SURVIVES. par's tail is uninitialised: +0x14 and +0x18 are zero because nothing ever wrote them, not because a constructor set them. That points at whatever should construct par - which is still unidentified, since sub_001F8830 constructs only the pool and takes par as an argument, meaning par already existed. (8) NEXT: par is passed in fully formed, so find its origin. It is the object whose vtable-bearing field0 record B18 holds {par, pool, 0x4000, allocator 01088A90}. Watch B18 itself, or find who allocates 0x1C bytes at 01091B30, rather than watching more of par's fields one at a time.

message: par's constructor found - sub_00202D14 - and it EXPLICITLY initialises the destroy gate to 0. My 'nothing initialises it' was wrong: the software poll detects CHANGES, not writes, so a field set to the value it already holds is invisible to it. par is six dwords, so +0x18 was never a field
note: (1) THE ORIGIN. Poll on par+0x00 gives one change, 0 -> 01091B18, from sub_00202D14+0x67C under the now-familiar chain sub_00123590 <- sub_00216EE0+0x2E8 <- sub_00222708 <- sub_002235D0 <- sub_002221E0 <- sub_00209650 <- sub_002366BC <- sub_0023666F <- sub_00239E50. Reading sub_00202D14 gives the whole construction: allocate 0x18 bytes through the allocator's vtbl+0xCC; par[0]=B18; par[4]=0 count; par[8]=0 seed; par[0xC]=0x400 capacity; allocate 0x1000 bytes for the array; par[0x10]=base; par[0x14]=0; then TAIL JUMP to sub_00202D89, which allocates 0x24 and constructs the pool. So one routine builds par, its array and the pool in sequence. (2) TWO EARLIER FINDINGS ARE CONFIRMED BY IT. The array allocation is 0x1000 bytes and the capacity is 0x400, which is 1024 entries of 4 bytes - independent confirmation that +0x0C counts ENTRIES, as the ordered-insert read concluded. And par is allocated at 0x18 bytes, i.e. SIX dwords ending at +0x14, so +0x18 was never a field at all. That is why nothing ever wrote it, and it is the fourth time this session that an offset past an object's end was mistaken for object state. (3) THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS. The previous entry said nothing in the binary initialises par+0x14. That is WRONG: its constructor sets it to 0 explicitly, three instructions after setting the base pointer. The gate's zero is deliberate. (4) WHY THE INSTRUMENT COULD NOT HAVE TOLD ME. The software poll compares the watched value against the last value it saw and reports a CHANGE. The memory was already zero when the constructor wrote zero to it, so there was no change and no report - the poll is structurally blind to an initialisation that matches the existing contents. This is a real limit of the instrument, distinct from the page watchpoint's problems, and it is now recorded: 'never written' can never be concluded from the poll alone. Read the constructor. (5) SO THE WALLS 40/41 LINK IS DEAD FOR A SECOND AND BETTER REASON. It is not an unpopulated container, and it is not an uninitialised field either. par[0x14] holds exactly what its constructor put there. (6) WHICH SHARPENS THE REAL QUESTION. sub_0020EEE0 reads `if (par[0x14] <= 0) { par[0x14]++; skip } else { unlink and free the pool }`. Starting from a deliberate 0, the first call is spared and the second destroys - that IS the original's design. So the defect is not the gate's value; it is that this path runs at all on the second of three block removals. sub_0020EF90 attempts a pool destroy on EVERY block whose refcount hits zero, gated only by MEM8(pool+0x20), which the pool constructor sets to 1 unconditionally. (7) NEXT: find what the gate is counting. Read every other reader of par+0x14 - not by offset grep, which has already produced two false leads, but by finding functions called with par as `this`. And establish whether sub_0020EF90 is meant to be reached from the refcount-zero path at all, since 66 registrations produced only 3 removals.

message: Exactly six functions ever operate on par, none through a vtable, and sub_0020EEE0 is the ONLY one that touches +0x14. The gate is private to the destroy path - so the defect is not the gate but that the destroy path runs per block at all
note: DIAGNOSTIC ONLY - the hook was reverted and a clean probe-free run reproduces the baseline exactly: 514 kernel calls, 445 callsites, crash sub_001EB890+0x1D5 (RVA 0xDEE205), fault 0x8B0146F4. (1) THE INSTRUMENT. Offset greps have produced two false leads on this wall, so instead of grepping, the call macros themselves were hooked: RECOMP_ABI_CALL logs #fn and RECOMP_ICALL_SAFE logs the target VA whenever g_ecx equals par. Registers are globals here (`#define ecx g_ecx`), so `this` is visible at every call site in the binary. Results deduped by name, giving the SET of functions that operate on the object rather than a trace. (2) THE COMPLETE SET, six functions: sub_001F8740, sub_001EB890 (the binary search and the crash site), sub_0020A360, sub_00204800 (the ordered insert), sub_001F87A0 (the name-lookup wrapper) and sub_0020EEE0 (the destroy). ZERO indirect calls were logged with par as this, which independently confirms par is non-polymorphic - consistent with it having no vtable and with its field0 being a plain record pointer. (3) THE DECISIVE PART: of those six, ONLY sub_0020EEE0 touches +0x14, and it both reads and writes it. The gate is private to the destroy path. Its whole life is: constructor sets it to 0, then sub_0020EEE0 reads it, skips on <=0 and increments, and destroys on anything higher. Nothing else in the binary participates. (4) SO THE GATE IS NOT THE DEFECT. It holds what its constructor put there and behaves as written: spare the first destroy request, honour every one after it. The bug is upstream - that a destroy request is issued at all for each block whose refcount reaches zero. sub_0020EF90 makes that request every time, gated only by MEM8(pool+0x20), which the pool constructor sets to 1 unconditionally. (5) HYPOTHESIS, NOT A FINDING, and the most promising one left: this whole teardown may be ERROR-PATH UNWINDING rather than normal operation. 66 classes are registered and only 3 are ever released, during static initialisation, long before anything would legitimately tear classes down, and the releases arrive through a recursive descent rooted at sub_001EA6B0. If that descent is unwinding from an earlier failure, wall 42 is a SYMPTOM and the real defect is whatever fails first. Testing that means finding what starts the descent, not further dissecting the pool. (6) NEXT: probe the entry of sub_001EA6B0 and walk up from there, and check whether the three released classes - igObject, igMetaField, igBoolMetaField - are related by inheritance, since those three being the ones torn down would suggest a specific registration failing rather than a general teardown.

message: THE TRIGGER: sub_001EA6B0 runs on 17 objects during DESCRIPTOR CREATION, and exactly ONE - 01098A40 - is processed TWICE, from two different callers. The three pool releases follow immediately. The error-unwinding hypothesis is refuted; this is the creation path
note: DIAGNOSIS ONLY - probes stripped, clean run reproduces the baseline: 514 kernel, 445 callsites, RVA 0xDEE205. (1) THE HYPOTHESIS FROM THE PREVIOUS ENTRY IS WRONG. I proposed the teardown might be error-path unwinding. It is not. Every sub_001EA6B0 invocation sits under sub_002096FD <- sub_0020E547 <- sub_002226E0 / sub_00214E20 <- sub_002235D0 - the descriptor CREATION machinery this project has already documented, with sub_0020E547 named in the ledger as the fatal call site. Objects are being built, not unwound. (2) SEVENTEEN INVOCATIONS, NOT SIX. The first probe used recomp_where with limit 6 and the process crashes before atexit, so the final-counts summary never printed and six looked like the total. A plain counting probe gives 17. A capped probe plus a summary that cannot run is indistinguishable from a complete result - the same trap the recomp_where header warns about, hit anyway. (3) THE FINDING. Of the 17 objects, sixteen are processed exactly once and ONE is processed twice: 01098A40, as entries #16 and #17. The three [REL] releases of pool 01092B58 occur on the very next lines. Nothing else in the run is processed twice. (4) IT IS NOT RECURSION. The two invocations arrive by DIFFERENT caller chains. #16: sub_001EA6B0 <- sub_002096FD <- sub_0020E547 <- sub_002226E0+0x111 <- sub_002235D0+0x524 <- sub_0021C110+0x12A <- sub_00209650+0x192. #17: sub_001EA6B0 <- sub_002096FD <- sub_0020E547 <- sub_00214E20+0x2D4 <- sub_00209650+0x37E <- sub_0021E190+0xA4 <- sub_00209470+0x47D. Two separate top-level calls on one object. #17's chain is the one that appeared in the original wall-42 backtraces, which confirms this is the invocation whose +0x620 frame sits above the releases. (5) INDEPENDENT CONFIRMATION THE PROBE WATCHES THE RIGHT MACHINERY: invocation #5 is this=01098358 - the fatal descriptor from TYPE_DESCRIPTOR.md - and its chain is sub_002226E0 <- sub_00223960 <- sub_002263F0, which is EXACTLY the path that document records for it ('reached through sub_00223960 -> FUN_002226e0, stored by sub_002263F0, which never sizes it'). Two independent investigations landing on the same path is worth something. Note 01098A40 and 01098358 share a vtable, 003F5D88, so they are the same class. (6) THE STORY THIS SUPPORTS, still a hypothesis: sub_001EA6B0 walks an object's metafields (its neighbour sub_001EA640 was read as exactly that), so running it twice on one object would release that object's field references twice, driving refcounts to zero early and triggering the pool destroy. That would make wall 42 a DOUBLE-RELEASE caused by double processing, not a defect in the pool code at all. (7) NEXT: find why 01098A40 is reached twice. The two chains diverge at sub_0020E547's caller - sub_002226E0 in one, sub_00214E20 in the other - so the question is which of those two is not supposed to run for this object, or what should have marked it already-processed between them.

message: WALL 42's DEFECT FOUND: 17 instances are created and 17 initialised, perfectly paired except the last - createInstance returns 01098938 and the initialiser then runs on 01098A40, the PREVIOUS instance. One object is left uninitialised and another is initialised twice, which is what double-releases the pool
note: DIAGNOSIS ONLY - probes stripped, clean run reproduces the baseline exactly: 514 kernel, 445 callsites, RVA 0xDEE205, fault 0x8B0146F4. (1) THE PAIRING.
